item.title: Trump’s anti-DEI movement comes for AI
item.description: Trump’s anti-DEI movement comes for AI
item.content:encoded:
Presented by NCTA - The Internet & Television Association: How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

Presented by 

The Department of Justice intervened in xAI's lawsuit challenging Colorado's AI law. | Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images

The legal crusade against affirmative action is coming for artificial intelligence.

On Friday, the Justice Department intervened in xAI’s challenge to Colorado’s “Consumer Protections for Artificial Intelligence” law. In its complaint, the DOJ argues the law’s provisions curbing algorithmic bias violates people’s 14th Amendment right to be treated equally under the law.

The intervention is in some ways an outgrowth of the movement to eradicate all race-conscious policies after the landmark Supreme Court case Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard in 2023 struck down affirmative action in college admissions.

Conservative groups like America First Legal, founded by now-White House adviser Stephen Miller, quickly seized on the decision to also challenge diversity initiatives in other contexts, like hiring and law journal recruiting. The DOJ took up that cause when President Donald Trump returned to office, and even cited the Harvard case in their challenge to the Colorado law.

This movement is now trying to beat back algorithmic bias laws, significantly narrowing the kinds of discrimination that the government is allowed to combat. Yet it’s unclear how successful these anti-DEI legal arguments will be in the context of machine learning, as opposed to admissions and hiring.

The Colorado law, in part, obligates developers to protect consumers from algorithmic discrimination, a phenomenon in which an AI model replicates biases in its training data. A key feature of the law is that it takes aim at disparate impact; a legal concept referring to instances in which an ostensibly neutral policy or system disadvantages a certain group of people — for example, job criteria that leads to disproportionately low minority hires.

The Trump administration has been trying to rid the legal system of the disparate impact concept in the wake of the Harvard case. The president released an executive order last year to eliminate disparate impact liability, contending the laws force businesses to engage in unconstitutional “racial balancing.” According to Andrew Selbst, a UCLA law professor, the DOJ complaint is aimed at bringing that effort into the realm of AI.

“They're trying to extend [the Harvard ruling] to do what Trump has said that he would do in that executive order and outlaw disparate impact,” said Selbst. “[The Colorado case] is just their vehicle to do it.”

Disparate impact does not need to be intentional, which is critical when it comes to the issue of algorithmic discrimination. There’s little evidence that developers generally intend for their AI to be biased. In other words, Colorado law says that developers have to address discrimination in algorithms for hiring, housing and other purposes even if the unequal impact is inadvertent.

Yet the DOJ argues in the complaint that such a law violates the 14th Amendment’s equal protection clause by distorting AI model outputs in a way that requires developers and deployers to discriminate based on race, sex, religion and other protected characteristics. It would be hard to meaningfully combat algorithmic discrimination if the government is only allowed to curb purposeful discrimination, according to Chicago-Kent College of Law professor Jason R. Bent, who studies AI and employment.

“The main concern is not that you're intentionally discriminating by setting the parameters in the algorithm based on the training data,” said Bent. “It's that it is going to reproduce, based on the training data, some existing biases or existing disparate outcome.”

So does trying to combat algorithmic discrimination amount to a 14th Amendment violation, similar to the way that it’s illegal to consider race in admissions? The courts haven’t decided on the question, but Bent and Selbst both said that machine learning introduces some unique complications.

Importantly, measures to address algorithmic discrimination mostly involve adjusting the training data. But because AI systems are opaque, it’s unclear whether they’re actually explicitly considering race in their decisionmaking in ways that courts have previously found to be illegal.

“You can have race consciousness in the actual design of the algorithm without ever having race play any part of the model in the actual decision process,” Selbst told DFD.

The Colorado attorney general’s office, which is being sued in xAI’s case, said it would not comment on ongoing litigation. The DOJ and xAI did not respond to inquiries.

Maine’s data center moratorium gets vetoed

Maine Gov. Janet Mills on Friday vetoed a bill that would have established the country’s first statewide moratorium on permits for data center construction.

In a letter to the Maine Legislature, Mills, a Democrat, wrote that she broadly supports a moratorium due to the impacts of data centers on utility prices and the environment in other states, but would not sign the bill because it didn’t include an exemption for a project in Jay, a Maine town that has weathered economic hardship after the closure of a local mill in 2023.

“After prior redevelopment efforts failed, the Town of Jay worked for two years on a $550 million data center redevelopment project to finally bring jobs and investment back to the mill site,” Mills wrote, adding that she would establish a council via executive order to evaluate the impact of data centers in Maine.

Musk and Altman to battle in court

Elon Musk and Sam Altman are finally going to trial OpenAI’s for-profit reorganization, Axel Springer’s Jacob Shamsian reports.

Jury selection started Monday to hear a fight over Musk’s claims that he contributed $40 million to OpenAI with the understanding it would stick to its nonprofit mission, but that Altman and other executives bypassed him to establish a for-profit arm. OpenAI argues that Musk knew the company needed to make a profit to be viable, and that his gripes are about not getting more control over the company.

The trial’s witness list has a bevy of heavy hitters, including Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and OpenAI’s former CTO Mira Murati. Jared Birchall, Musk’s right-hand man, may also testify.

item.title: The leftist data center argument
item.description: The leftist data center argument
item.content:encoded:
Presented by NCTA - The Internet & Television Association: How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

Presented by 

With help from Makayla Gray and Hassan Kanu

A new Jacobin op-ed argues that the left's support for data center moratoriums is misguided. | Mario Tama/Getty Images

The socialist magazine Jacobin ran an op-ed on Sunday arguing that the left is making a serious mistake in backing data center moratoriums. The piece has sparked a fiery debate among liberals as the Democratic party figures out its stance on data centers and affordability ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. 

Holly Buck, an associate environment and sustainability professor at the University of Buffalo, writes that such moratoriums could exacerbate the class divides the left wants to minimize. She contends that the policies may lead to data center offshoring, which raises prices on AI services and limits access for economically disadvantaged users. Instead, Buck proposes that the left focus on policies that enable more people to democratically govern AI. DFD spoke to Buck about the reactions to her piece, and the class dynamics of the data center backlash.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity. 

Why do you think data center moratoriums have become increasingly associated with the political left? 

Environmental groups might have seen this issue as a way to have something energizing that's a win. There's been a tension from them, not just from that instrumental standpoint, but also that people are really concerned about the impacts on both climate and local impacts on water. You have all of that concern and it finds an outlet in something that has momentum. People are also concerned about AI more broadly in terms of impacts on social life, learning and the economy.

Your Jacobin op-ed is focused on equity, but that concept has a lot of different facets: Labor, affordability, access, the environment. How do you think about these tradeoffs to conclude that moratoriums are, on balance, bad for equity? 

I am worried about access to AI. I teach a class about how to use generative AI, and I'm seeing these students come up with amazing pieces of work that are helping them think about solving environmental challenges. I see [the technology] as a useful thing that I want people to have access to. I don't want that to just be people at large companies who have access to these capabilities. The other equity dimension that I'm concerned about is the prospect of offshoring data centers to places with less environmental regulation and governance protections. This is a trend we have seen with a whole bunch of industries.

Is it possible that AI companies will just keep prices high regardless of whether the data centers are offshored? Is offshoring really a major driver of price?

Constraints on compute are going to impact the prices. That’s not a sophisticated economic analysis. It's just a basic supply and demand observation.

What do you make of the reaction and discourse this piece has sparked?

The proposition that there are class dynamics to the backlash seems to have drawn the most attention. I’m making an observation that we don't actually know that much about the class dynamics in terms of a peer-reviewed social science sense. If we have a situation where middle- and upper- class people are more engaged — in part because it is challenging for people who are working to do a lot of public participation — there's a couple of potential implications in that it could slow the development of the infrastructure before people have had a chance to work with and learn from these models.

What if studies find the opposite: that the backlash is from the working class. Would that change the equation for you?

If more data emerges that this is really a working-class movement, I would revisit some of these arguments and keep other ones. But it's not just about who the people are showing up to meetings. It's also about who is funding this backlash, bankrolling the organizing and profiting from the conflict that needs to be examined — not only the people on the ground.

What’s your response to the argument that a moratorium would give us time to establish policies for democratic governance?

There's some ways in which the buying time argument makes sense, especially in jurisdictions where they just don't have the planning capacity. But overall, there are some places where this buying time argument falls short. The thing that is unique about AI is that there are some dynamics of a race here. I wish there weren't, but I think that's real. The moratorium also doesn't facilitate the long-term goals because the elements of the coalition that are pushing for the moratorium are going to have different positions on what the long-term picture should be.

What do you make of the labor displacement concerns that are partly driving the left’s support for data center moratoriums?

The challenge with AI is that the potential for the redistribution of wealth to these tech companies is so huge. It's a moment where I do think there is leverage, and I sympathize with the argument that the threat of a moratorium. I think the threat of a moratorium in Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s bill was meant to be a signal to the tech industry. I agree with them broadly that this is a moment to renegotiate the social contract

My challenge to the left is that we can do so much more with this moment than revisit the politics of blocking infrastructure and try to treat this as a local zoning issue.

Saikat Chakrabarti dishes on his AI plan

Saikat Chakrabarti, one of the four Democrats looking to replace Rep. Nancy Pelosi when she retires, unveiled his AI platform today in an interview with POLITICO’s Makayla Gray.

His plan calls for job guarantees for workers displaced by the technology, a 32-hour work week, a publicly owned national AI lab and a requirement that data centers cover their own electricity.

Chakrabarti says he wants to focus less on regulating the technology, and more on who makes the decisions controlling it. His plan comes amid growing concerns in both parties about how AI could lead to mass job loss and economic disruption.

“Public First, the Anthropic-backed super PAC, is committed to spending whatever it takes to defeat me, because they want to be in control entirely where this technology goes and do the bare minimum on regulation so they can keep going pretty much unchecked,” said Chakrabarti, a former engineer at Stripe.

Public First has said it plans to spend heavily to support Chakrabarti’s opponent, Sen. Scott Wiener. Former Rep. Brad Carson, who leads the PAC, previously said the super PAC network will spend whatever it takes for Wiener to win, citing the lawmaker’s authorship of California AI laws.

Chakrabarti says his plan has the potential to be stronger in implementing AI regulation than SB 53, an AI bill that his opponent state Sen. Scott Wiener introduced, saying it made no meaningful checks to regulation of AI.

“If that's the route we go, which is the route that I think a lot of the Public First kind of candidates are pitching, that's going to be disastrous,” Chakrabarti said. “It’s going to be the AI version of greenwashing.” The plan also calls for making a new AI trust fund, paid for by imposed taxes on AI companies.

A federal court has approved an agreement pausing a lawsuit challenging Colorado’s algorithmic discrimination law, POLITICO’s Hassan Kanu reports for DFD.

Weiser explained in the joint request that his office won’t enforce the law until after the current legislative session due to “the possibility that legislation replacing or amending SB24-205 will be enacted” during the current session. 

A magistrate judge granted the parties’ request on Monday. xAI and the Colorado AG did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

item.title: The AI arms race’s sneakiest tactic
item.description: The AI arms race’s sneakiest tactic
item.content:encoded:
Presented by NCTA - The Internet & Television Association: How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

Presented by 

A US and a Chinese flag wave outside a commercial building in Beijing, 09 July 2007. | Teh Eng Koon/AFP via Getty Images

The White House has sounded the alarm on a high-tech ploy that’s allowed developers in China to piggyback off American AI labs.

Last week, the Office of Technology and Science Policy Director Michael Kratsios released a memo reporting that Chinese entities have been conducting “industrial-scale campaigns to distill U.S. frontier AI systems.”

Distillation is a training technique that involves a “student” model submitting a series of inquiries to a “teacher” model in order to replicate its performance. Though it does have legitimate uses, Kratsios wrote that some actors are abusing the process: “Leveraging tens of thousands of proxy accounts to evade detection and using jailbreaking techniques to expose proprietary information, these coordinated campaigns systematically extract capabilities from American AI models, exploiting American expertise and innovation.”

While unauthorized distillation is a technical problem that demands technical solutions, diplomacy could also help to curb the practice. The government has tools at its disposal to discourage China’s AI developers from plundering American models, and foreign policy analysts say shrewd strategy could go a long way to help curtail the problem.

“Creating a [distillation] taboo requires a mix of diplomacy, creating international forums, and it has to have some compliance costs,” Benjamin Jensen, a senior fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies who previously testified before Congress on distillation, told DFD. “What would be the right mix of sanctions or entity list designations that would be part of longer-term economic statecraft policy?”

One challenge with addressing distillation is the legal gray area around it, especially when it comes to criminal liability. While many companies prohibit the practice in their terms of service, distillation typically involves going through the front door to submit queries to publicly available models, rather than traditional hacking.

“The closest [applicable criminal statute] is the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, and it may be that the Department of Justice is able to prosecute under that statute,” said Joe Khawam, a managing director at the Law Reform Institute who was formerly an attorney in the State Department’s Office of the Legal Adviser. “However, criminal prosecutions take time, and many of the actors won't be subject to U.S. jurisdiction, so whether or not criminal statutes will serve as an effective deterrence is a real question.”

Even absent a viable criminal prosecution strategy, there are trade and diplomacy laws that could exact economic consequences for distillation. Yet given the U.S.’s already fraught relations with China, attempting to restrain distillation may require a delicate approach. Khawam has proposed a strategy to gradually ratchet up the pressure on China.

The approach begins with imposing export licensing requirements on major Chinese AI labs, which would restrict their access to American chips if they conduct distillation campaigns. If that activity doesn’t cease, then the escalation would continue until it reaches the most extreme option of freezing the labs’ U.S. assets and prohibiting Americans from dealing with them — which is how the government handles narcotics traffickers and terrorists.

According to Khawam, immediately jumping to the harshest sanctions would run the risk of Beijing retaliating with its trump card: critical minerals. China produces 90 percent of the world’s critical minerals, which are essential for everything from consumer tech devices to robotics, so cutting off access would be devastating for U.S. industry. “The hope certainly would be that sanctions wouldn't be necessary, that bilateral diplomacy would be sufficient, but of course you want to have that stick in case it is needed,” Khawam told DFD.

Another way to avoid a retaliatory tit-for-tat would be to get more countries involved in collectively agreeing that unauthorized distillation is bad form, said Jensen. Having more actors involved could defray the impact of potential retaliation from China, but it also just establishes a norm. “So by shining a light, by bringing in other countries, you're bringing a reputational risk to bear for the perpetrators,” Jensen told DFD. “So that's where you actually do get good diplomatic forums.”

But before going through all this trouble and risking a further strain on relations with China, Georgetown Center for Security and Emerging Technology research associate Kyle Miller says a crucial question still needs to be answered: How much has distillation actually helped Chinese labs advance their models?

“Let's assume … they get a slight bump in performance — in that case, it’s fine that we invest in some defenses on the margins,” he told DFD. The threat could be largely left for the industry to address on its own. If it’s a significant driver of China’s AI progress, then some of these more aggressive government measures would be warranted.

“If distillation is very effective and it's giving Chinese companies a major performance bump, that implies that a lot of China's frontier AI capabilities are dependent on distillation of U.S. models,” Miller told DFD.

Anthropic pointed DFD to its report on distillation, and to company policy head Sarah Heck’s statement on the OSTP memo: “We need to have more of a spotlight on this issue, and look forward to continuing to collaborate on maintaining American AI leadership.” OpenAI pointed DFD to a memo on distillation it sent to the China Select Committee in February. The White House and the Chinese embassy in D.C. did not respond to inquiries.

King Charles boosts a tech deal

King Charles III’s visit to Washington may help to revive the United Kingdom’s Tech Prosperity Deal with the U.S., POLITICO’s Joseph Bambridge reports.

“Our new partnerships in nuclear fusion and quantum computing and in A.I. and life sciences” could save “countless lives,” the king said in his Tuesday address to Congress. The TDP would establish a U.S.-U.K. joint effort across the AI, quantum and civil nuclear sectors.

He later attended a reception with tech executives from firms including Nvidia and Google, where he told attendees “there is no limit to what we can achieve” through collaboration between the U.S. and the U.K.

The British embassy in Washington said in a statement concerning the TDP that the reception was meant to “galvanise confidence in the UK as a tier-one partner for technology cooperation and reaffirm the depth of the commercial and scientific ties that underpin it.” The Trump administration froze talks on the TDP due to broader trade disagreements in December, and the U.K. has been trying to restart the negotiations since February.

item.title: How Mythos could upend the economics of hacking
item.description: How Mythos could upend the economics of hacking
item.content:encoded:
Presented by NCTA - The Internet & Television Association: How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

Presented by 

AI models like Mythos could make hacking a lot cheaper. | Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP via Getty Images

Despite Hollywood depictions of lone-wolf hackers breaking into secure systems from a bedroom, high-tech subterfuge typically requires access to significant financial resources and help from partners.

Yet based on recent reports from Anthropic, its powerful new Mythos model could significantly lower the resources required for hacking.

Mythos has set off a wave of anxiety across government and the private sector due to its purported ability to identify previously unknown vulnerabilities in major operating systems and web browsers.

Anthropic’s findings suggest that Mythos could slash the labor and computing costs required to exploit cybersecurity gaps. It’s a major revelation given that the roughly $250 billion cybersecurity industry has made hacking an expensive enterprise. If Anthropic’s claims are accurate, then Mythos is poised to upend the economics of cybersecurity.

“We used to be able to impose costs on the attackers, which made it hard for them to do their job,” said Grady Summers, CEO of the data security firm Netwrix. “Mythos is discovering these vulnerabilities that no one's found before, and the damage is even bigger than that because it's making the cost for the attacker so cheap that they can retool quicker or iterate faster.”

Breaching a government or large corporate system has traditionally involved paying elite hackers to spend a lot of time figuring out a way in, according to Summers. That’s why nation-states often bankroll the most notorious hacking groups.

“A lot of these advanced persistent threat groups that have been exposed over the years [had] actual financial capital, offices, significant compute infrastructure,” Summers told DFD. “It's just crazy to think in 10 minutes [using AI] I could do the work that might have taken an advanced threat group months to do.”

A notable finding from Anthropic’s preliminary testing of Mythos, which has sparked both shock and doubts, is that the model was able to identify a 27-year-old vulnerability in a popular security software package through a series of tests totaling $20,000. (The particular test run that found the bug cost only $50.)

Isaac Evans, CEO of the code security company Semgrep, told DFD that finding the bug would cost “at least” as much without AI, and that the price tag will continue to drop as models advance. “The models will only get cheaper and human labor costs will only get more expensive,” he said.

Evans added that companies and governments likely wouldn’t have paid cybersecurity professionals tens of thousands of dollars to find that kind of vulnerability in the past, since it would’ve been less likely for human hackers to identify it. But there may be more incentive to shell out now if hackers are using AI. “Everyone knows there are tons of vulnerabilities in our core infrastructure,” he said. “It just hasn't been worth it to pay people to go and find them.”

While Mythos’ ability to find unknown cracks in cybersecurity systems has attracted a lot of attention, less advanced models may make other aspects of hacking quicker and cheaper. Hackers often try to trick senior officials and company executives with phony emails and websites, and AI can help craft those phishing ploys.

“You'd have to get [a senior target’s] email address, you'd research their social media, LinkedIn … personal information about the victim” Summers told DFD. “It helps you do that so much quicker, and I can now come up with a dozen different variations [of phishing messages] in perfect English.”

These cost and time savings for hackers don’t necessarily translate to equally lower costs for defenders, according to both Summers and Evans, so AI is likely to shift the market equilibrium for cybersecurity. Hackers can use AI to throw everything at the wall and see what sticks, whereas it can be harder to predict all the possible attacks from a defense perspective.

“This just really favors attackers and I think it means that organizations will actually have to meaningfully increase their security spend,” said Evans. “There is now a phenomenally easy capability [that’s] maybe a hundred times cheaper to develop exploits against just the average American corporation.”

Anthropic did not respond to an inquiry.

The U.S. dings Vietnam on IP

The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative accused Vietnam in a new report of failing to safeguard intellectual property rights, POLITICO’s Ari Hawkins writes.

In its annual review of global IP enforcement, the agency labeled Vietnam a “priority foreign country” — the most serious classification. This marks the first time in more than a decade that the U.S. has imposed the designation on a trading partner. USTR now has 30 days to open a formal investigation under the Trade Act of 1974, which could lead to restrictions like tariffs.

“This identification follows extensive bilateral engagement between the United States and Vietnam that has failed to resolve long-standing concerns regarding IP protection and enforcement,” the report reads. “Although Vietnam has taken some enforcement actions, these efforts are insufficient to address the full range of serious concerns.”

Critics have alleged that the decision is actually aimed at suppressing speech, since the FCC’s order was released the day after President Donald Trump and Melania Trump called on ABC to fire Jimmy Kimmel for joking that the first lady had a “glow like an expectant widow."

However, Carr is claiming the review was sparked by an investigation into Disney’s diversity, equity and inclusion practices. “This is a decision that we made inside this building, based on where we were in the enforcement matter,” Carr said during a Thursday press conference. “There was no pressure from the outside. item.description: David Sacks talks Anthropic
item.content:encoded:
Presented by NCTA - The Internet & Television Association: How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

Presented by 

David Sacks was the Trump administration's former AI and crypto czar, and currently co-chairs the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology. | AP

Former White House AI and crypto czar David Sacks, who currently co-chairs the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, talked about Anthropic’s turbulent dealings with the administration in an exclusive interview with POLITICO’s Dasha Burns this week. In the interview, portions of which are reproduced below, Sacks discusses Anthropic’s ongoing conflict with the administration concerning the company’s insistence that the Pentagon not use its technology for mass domestic surveillance and fully autonomous weapons targeting. He also talks about how the AI startup's powerful new Mythos model may trigger a cybersecurity arms race that will ultimately lead to more secure digital systems. You can watch a video of the conversation here, and listen to it here. 

This interview has been edited for clarity and length. 

Is the feud with Anthropic over? Are all agencies going to be free to keep using the company's products in perpetuity? And what do you make of that government-versus-AI narrative?

I think that if you're an AI company and you don't want your product to be used in war, then don't sell to the Department of War. But they did make a decision that they wanted to be used by the Department of War. They made that decision and then they tried to insert themselves in the chain of command by having a veto over the lawful uses of their product.

I was not involved in the Anthropic dispute with the Pentagon. I'm still not involved in it, but if you want my opinion, I just don't think it was a very realistic position for them to take to say that they can dictate to a government agency what lawful uses of their product should be allowed. I think you have to make a decision about whether you're going to sell to that government agency or not.

I do think they did try to set themselves up in a way of being superior to the chain of command. I think that that's a tough position to take with respect to any government department, but particularly with respect to the Pentagon.

One of their concerns was around mass surveillance. First of all, the Pentagon says that it does not engage in that, and that's not a lawful use. If [Anthropic] had come to me as a policy matter and said, "Hey, we have all these concerns about loopholes in the law. We want to ensure greater privacy for Americans,” I would've been very interested in having that conversation.

[Anthropic] recently announced Mythos as this new cybersecurity tool, which it says has unprecedented hacking capabilities and is too dangerous to release publicly. How big of a national security threat is this?

I think ultimately if everyone does what they're supposed to do, it won't be a national security threat. We have this area of cybersecurity where you've got the white hats versus the black hats, and basically, it's all about preventing hackers from breaching systems. They try to break in. They try to steal data. Maybe plant back doors, do other nefarious things. You have this arms race between cyber offense and cyber defense. AI is going to be a major part of cybersecurity moving forward, meaning that you're going to have hackers who are powered up by AI models, but then you've got cyber defenders who are powered up by AI capabilities as well.

So public access to Mythos you don't think is as big of a national security concern?

No, no. Listen, holding it back was the right decision, because I would not want the hackers to have access to it before the defenders. What I'm saying is that I believe that the market will eventually reach a new equilibrium, in which there are AI capabilities on the part of both hackers and then also cyber defense. AI is going to solve the problem that AI creates.

That sounds like the tagline for your AI theory: AI will solve the problems AI creates.

It may not solve every problem, but I do think in the case of hacking it will. Mythos is a good example. They're giving limited access or preview to a couple of dozen companies and the government, and what the people who are in this Project Glasswing will do is they're going to use the capabilities to scan their code bases, look for vulnerabilities and then patch them.

Ultimately, Mythos isn't the only AI model that will do this. All the major AI companies are working on this now. It's really an extension of coding capabilities. I think the net result of it is that we're going to find a lot of dormant vulnerabilities that were there in the software, maybe for a long time, that no one had found before. As long as everyone does what they're supposed to do — which is the [chief information security officers] and the IT departments use these new tools to patch the bugs — then actually it will harden cybersecurity around our core systems because those vulnerabilities won't be there anymore.

item.title: The push to audit AI systems
item.description: The push to audit AI systems
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

AI auditing can help to address bias in technologies like facial recognition. | David McNew/AFP via Getty Images

Alondra Nelson served as the acting director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy under President Joe Biden, was a key architect of that administration’s seminal Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights, and now leads the Science, Technology, and Social Values Lab at the Institute for Advanced Study. The social science professor is the co-author of a new book, Auditing AI, which examines the process of testing models to evaluate the risk of bias and other potential harms. She talks to us about why evaluating AI models isn’t just for computer scientists, and the Trump administration’s concern about ideologically biased models. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

There are a lot of potential safeguards for AI use. Why did you want to focus on auditing?

The audit is not the only tool in our arsenal, but it's a very important one. It's important because we're living at a time when AI systems are already involved in our lives, making consequential decisions about who gets a kidney transplant, who gets bail, who gets a job interview, whether or not a family in a certain demographic gets housing. We're looking at autonomous weapon systems that are deployed on battlefields today

These are not hypothetical future risks. These are things that are happening right now, and they're happening at scale with almost no systematic or public oversight. The audit … is a really powerful tool for accountability.

What kinds of actors do you think are well-positioned to conduct these audits?

You want people who are technically skilled. But there's a group of us who are co-authors of this book, and they include several computer scientists, but also folks with expertise in the law, social scientists, a journalist. What we're trying to signal as a group of co-authors is that you actually don't need highly technical expertise to do an audit. Not that you don't need any, but you don't need to have a PhD in computer science to be able to look at what a system says it's supposed to be doing or how it's supposed to be acting, and to take a systematic look at an AI [model’s] behavior.

How do you define what exactly bias is in AI? What does a fair, unbiased model look like?

“Bias” has a technical definition, which is just to say that your input data is always going to be constrained. You're not going to have, in most cases, a fully representative set of input data. That will always constrain the types of outputs that you can have. Where we sometimes get confused is that that gets layered over with what we think about as bias in society — which might include racial or other forms of discrimination.

Sometimes it's certainly the case that there's an interplay between the two — using a database that's historically biased will have outcomes that are particularly biased toward groups of individuals who are seeking a job, a mortgage loan, etc. There are both social and technical definitions. What auditing AI is really interested in, and where it's useful, is the overlay between those two. So what you might think of as a sociotechnical understanding of bias that's both about the technical limitations, and then [about] when technically biased tools are deployed in the real world and the implications that they variously have for people's lives.

The book focuses a lot on AI that’s biased against protected identity groups. What do you think about the idea of auditing for political bias, which the Trump administration has been interested in?

Where I certainly agree with the Trump administration is in that technical space: All AI systems are biased, and auditing is [how] you find out the ways in which they are biased.

When you get into what the Trump administration calls “ideological bias,” that gets a little bit harder to measure. If the desired outcome is that everyone gets treated the same, what does that look like ideologically? One would want to drive a line at consequences for people's lives that would violate civil liberties, civil rights law, privacy law and the like.

Some states, like New York, and the European Union have regulations requiring AI audits. Do they seem satisfactory? 

The U.K. continues to have the most developed institutional, organizational infrastructure for [auditing and] doing assessments of AI models. But this is just the very beginning, and one of the things that we're trying to stress with releasing this book is that we're going to have to figure out times when we will get auditing wrong, or it'll catch some things and not other things, or we won't scale it in the right way. But all of the questions that we might want to ask … can only be addressed by actually starting to do the process. We still need the wherewithal, the funding and the institutional collaboration to build out the system.

There’s a lot of concern about hampering AI development in the U.S. How do you think about designing audits that don’t stifle innovation? Do we necessarily have to accept some amount of harm? 

Auditing comes at the end. The tool is completed and it's about to be deployed, or it has been deployed. Auditing is not interfering in the development pathway of the technology. Auditing is this gut check that says, “This is what you say the tool does. Does it actually do it?” If you're very worried about there being strong trade-offs with innovation — which I think is a little bit of red herring — then certainly auditing is something that you want to turn to because of where it comes in the development pipeline.

We're not going to prevent all the harms. But right now we're not doing anything. There's little risk in getting this wrong if we're going from doing nothing at all to doing a little bit, and maybe missing a few things.

A divide is emerging among Democrats heading into the midterm elections over whether to narrowly focus on the pocket-book costs of data centers or to push for industry regulations more broadly, POLITICO’s Calder McHugh and Riley Rogerson report.

There is general agreement among Democrats that scrutinizing data centers fits neatly with the party’s plan to run on affordability in the midterm elections. “There’s a large contingent within the Democratic Party that maintains a posture that Democrats won when they had the backing of Silicon Valley, and we need to get them back,” said a Democratic strategist working on AI issues, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly about strategy. “Not only is that objectively misguided, but … a strategy of appeasement is unlikely to be successful. If we want Silicon Valley to pay attention to us, they need to be scared of us and believe there’s a real chance regulation is coming.”

Fish inspire Air Force AI

item.title: A potential AI labor lesson from China
item.description: A potential AI labor lesson from China
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

Chinese courts have recently ruled that companies cannot terminate workers due to AI. | Adek Berry/AFP via Getty Images

Two legal rulings are undercutting a bedrock premise of the AI “race” with China, and they didn’t come from the U.S.

A Hangzhou court ruled last week that it was illegal for a company to demote then dismiss a senior tech worker and replace him with artificial intelligence, the second such decision to come from the country’s courts since December. The decision comes as China moves to disseminate the technology across several industries at breakneck speed, and as its companies look to automate their operations.

Some experts say the rulings undercut a core argument in the U.S. that implementing forceful safeguards on artificial intelligence will cause the nation to lose the AI race with China.

“[The rulings] blow the China competition argument out of the water,” said Darrell West, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution. “This is an example of China being tougher on tech companies than is the case in the United States, so the idea that America should not regulate technology because it'll hurt us with China is completely negated by this legal action.”

The rulings come as China faces political and economic challenges that are pushing it to move more aggressively to stymie AI labor displacement, according to Center for a New American Security research associate Ruby Scanlon.

The country has long relied on citizens’ acceptance of one-party rule to assure their quality of life and prosperity, yet AI threatens to upend the population’s well-being.

“[China] just can’t tolerate macro instability in the way that a democracy can,” Scanlon told DFD. “When the system is shaken even a little bit, it’s susceptible to break.”

China’s labor market is already in a tough position, and AI threatens to make it worse. Deflation and general pessimism around economic opportunities have partly led the country’s young adult unemployment rates to surge. Government debt and flagging household spending have put the public on edge about the broader economy as well.

“Because of the economic situation that China is already in with its debt, less consumer demand and high youth unemployment, [AI labor displacement] is just especially scary to them,” said Scanlon.

The prospect of AI replacing workers is alarming Americans, given already dwindling employment numbers. So shouldn’t the U.S. also put a hard limit on companies’ ability to replace workers with AI?

Well, making this a rule in the U.S. would require strong political will to overhaul longstanding employment laws. The country is an outlier in how much latitude it gives to employers over terminations.

The default at the federal level and in every state except Montana is at-will employment, which allows companies to dismiss workers for almost any legal reason. Bargaining contracts often have just-cause provisions that narrow the circumstances in which companies can let workers go. Prohibiting AI-related layoffs would likely require legislation that applies these provisions more broadly, and that stipulates that the technology does not constitute just cause for dismissal, according to Cornell labor law professor Gali Racabi.

“[Such legislation] is very, very far from where we are now,” said Racabi, who added that this kind of effort would take “extreme political will that is absent in most states and localities.”

But if such legislation were to pass someday, it might be a boon for AI growth. Peter Michael Lazes, who works on labor issues as co-coordinator of Penn State’s Healthcare Partnership initiative, contends that such measures could actually accelerate AI adoption. He suggested that workers may be more willing to use AI tools if they know the technology isn’t going to replace them. Employers would also have an incentive to train workers in AI in order to place them in new positions, rather than laying them off, Lazes added.

“If we had the political will to do this, it would harness the effectiveness of AI so that it is not only helpful to the stakeholders, but also to the shareholders,” he told DFD. “If China can do it, why can’t we?”

item.title: Why AI vetting is freaking people out
item.description: Why AI vetting is freaking people out
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

The White House is considering an executive order that would, in part, require government pre-approval for releasing frontier AI models. | Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP

The prospect of the government vetting AI models is causing a minor panic in certain tech policy and industry circles.

This week, the New York Times and POLITICO reported that the White House is considering an executive order that would, in part, require government testing and approval before AI companies can release their models.

Kevin Hassett then said during a Wednesday Fox Business appearance that the executive order may include “a clear roadmap to everybody about … how future AIs that also potentially create vulnerabilities should go through a process so that they’re released to the wild after they’ve been proven safe, just like an FDA drug.”

The news came as the administration met with tech companies about Mythos and other AI models that potentially pose a dire threat to cybersecurity. Such a proposal for the government to pre-approve model releases has received opposition from free-market think tanks and industry-aligned tech policy advisers, along with some academics.

Much of the debate speaks to a question that any policymaker faces when trying to regulate a potentially harmful product: Do you try to ensure something is safe before it’s released, or punish companies after the fact if something goes wrong?

When it comes to tech regulation, the U.S. has traditionally favored the latter approach of imposing penalties after a product causes harm in the wild.

“It gets to what is the heart and soul of America's technological governance regime, which is that we have a regime for computing and digital communication that's much more ex-post and responsive in character,” said Adam Thierer, a resident senior fellow at the R Street Institute.

There are plenty of reasons to think that going to the other extreme of requiring government pre-approval would be a bad idea for AI.

“Frankly, it would create a false sense of security,” said Neil Chilson, a former acting chief technologist at the Federal Trade Commission who is currently the Abundance Institute's head of AI policy. “There's only so much you can do in a lab environment … to actually study something that is a general-purpose technology, that is going to be deployed in lots of different spaces.”

Getting upfront government approval could be an issue if it leads people to be less vigilant about problems after release. “You also want to be continuing to iterate and modify and monitor after that release,” said Encode General Counsel Nathan Calvin.

Given the notoriously glacial pace of bureaucracy, waiting on the government to give the green light could slow innovation, but also make it harder for public watchdogs to conduct their own oversight.

“A lot of the most concerning risks from frontier models come from how they are used internally within the companies that develop them,” Helen Toner, interim executive director at the Georgetown Center for Security and Emerging Technology, told DFD. “Creating extra barriers to releasing them would do nothing to solve that problem, and would lengthen the time period when companies have advanced models internally that the public — and independent experts — have no access to.”

And if you consider models to have some elements of speech, then there could be constitutional issues with a pre-approval regime. The First Amendment forbids “prior restraint,” which involves requiring government authorization before something can be expressed. American laws around defamation or obscenity are designed to punish illicit speech after the fact. Prohibiting prior restraint is a core tenet of First Amendment law, born out of a history of censors attempting to control printing presses. Thierer suggests that having the government oversee model releases could run afoul of this principle.

“Information communication technologies have special First Amendment concerns … when you regulate them,” he said. “If you're regulating a model to be ‘safe,’ that can be done along certain dimensions where you could probably try to avoid getting into speech concerns, but at some point you might.”

Yet if models like Mythos are as powerful as companies claim, then waiting for harm to occur could result in a catastrophe that’s hard to mitigate. Even so, Toner suggests that looping in regulators on an advisory level prior to release could be a preferable alternative to giving them veto power. “[I]t obviously would have been better for CISA to have early access to Mythos and be actively working to coordinate cyber defense among U.S. critical infrastructure providers,” she said.

This is more aligned with the approach of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at the Commerce Department. The agency announced deals with Microsoft, xAI and Google DeepMind on Tuesday to conduct pre-deployment evaluations, though this is done on a voluntary basis. Chilson was supportive of the idea: “[Companies] don't always have all of the context for what the government might know about our adversaries or what they might know about our own governmental systems.”

A White House official told DFD on background: “Any policy announcement will come directly from the President. Discussion about potential executive orders is speculation.”

European tech companies are concerned that a new law reducing reliance on American cloud services has glaring loopholes, POLITICO’s Mathieu Pollet reports.

The European Commission has been crafting regulations to promote the domestic cloud industry as concerns mount over the bloc’s reliance on U.S. data and digital infrastructure. However, some companies fear the law could still allow American cloud companies to maintain their grip on Europe. Frank Karlitschek, the CEO of German provider Nextcloud, said he anticipates the law will have “a little nice exception at the end” permitting the use of American services if there are no viable European alternatives.

The commission just awarded cloud contracts last month to a joint venture that includes Google. “This is an open door for Microsoft, Amazon — everybody,” said Francisco Mingorance, secretary-general of European cloud lobby group CISPE.

item.description: How antitrust law could weaken AI security
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

AI companies like OpenAI have reported weathering distillation attacks. | Kiichiro Sato/AP

Antitrust law could threaten to hobble AI labs’ attempts to stop foreign developers from pilfering their technology.

Anthropic, OpenAI and Google all released strikingly similar reports earlier this year of Chinese developers launching distillation attacks — a high-tech maneuver for extracting key information to train other models. Distillation involves a “student” model submitting a large number of prompts to a “teacher” model to figure out what’s going on under the hood.

White House Office of Science and Technology Policy Director Michael Kratsios then published a memo late last month disclosing that the government has evidence of Chinese entities conducting “industrial-scale campaigns to distill U.S. frontier AI systems.” (The Chinese embassy in Washington previously told DFD that the allegations are “groundless.”)

The Trump administration wants AI companies to work together to combat Chinese efforts to extract sensitive model information. But antitrust experts and AI policy analysts say vague competition laws may discourage such coordination, creating a potential conflict between Washington’s national security priorities and antitrust regulations.

Kratsios laid out the administration’s game plan to combat unauthorized distillation in his memo, which will include an effort to “[e]nable the private sector to better coordinate against such attacks.”

Teamwork between companies to address this threat might seem like common sense, but making it happen isn’t all that straightforward. Bloomberg recently reported that AI companies have limited the information they share about distillation attacks due to fear of violating antitrust laws. Fair competition is important for AI, given how quickly it’s reshaping consumers’ lives.

“The most obvious thing the U.S. government should do at the moment is to facilitate information sharing between AI labs,” said Kyle Miller, a research analyst at Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology. “The companies are just concerned that … it could be interpreted as anti-competitive behavior, and they just want the government to squash those concerns.”

The Sherman Antitrust Act, which is the bedrock of American competition law, prohibits companies from conspiring together to unduly restrain the market. That rule has traditionally been applied to prevent companies from price-fixing or ganging up on a competitor with a joint boycott.

Yet it’s not entirely clear how foundational antitrust laws like the Sherman Act, many of which were enacted more than 100 years ago, apply to industry coordination on modern technologies like AI. That uncertainty discourages AI labs from alerting each other to IP addresses associated with distillation attacks or large-scale campaigns, Miller told DFD.

“Unlike some areas of law that the companies have to deal with … antitrust doesn't have a detailed set of regulations that you could just analyze and point to the provision saying that what you want to do is okay or isn't okay,” said Tim Schnabel, president of the Law Reform Institute. “A lot of the analysis is very fact-intensive, so every time the companies want to work together on some new issue, they have to spin up their lawyers.”

Antitrust laws allow for cooperation on certain matters, but determining whether companies can do so involves a sometimes nebulous analysis of whether the benefits of the activity outweigh the anti-competitive impacts.

According to Lily Li, an AI risk attorney who founded the tech-focused firm Metaverse Law, sharing technical details on threats like distillation would likely pass muster, as long as it doesn't include anything related to “go-to-market strategies, pricing models or vendor pricing.” Such security information shouldn’t have a direct impact on consumer prices.

Yet, there hasn’t been a definitive signal from the government that companies won’t expose themselves to antitrust liability for working together on the issue. The Law Reform Institute recently called on the Department of Justice and the Federal Trade Commission to provide guidance on what AI risk information can be shared.

Distillation is only one issue for which some sort of collaboration could be important. Risks relating to the use of AI for developing bioweapons and other catastrophic threats may also be mitigated if labs join forces. Relatedly, OpenAI actually has a line in its charter stating: “[I]f a value-aligned, safety-conscious project comes close to building AGI before we do, we commit to stop competing with and start assisting this project.”

Schnabel told DFD that such a commitment is an even thornier prospect, since it goes beyond info sharing or limited security-related collaboration. Yet he noted that it still might be a good idea, despite the possible antitrust implications.

“There's something to be said for there being a real public interest in how this technology develops so that it's not merely a race,” Schnabel said.

“No single AI lab can address this [distillation] threat alone,” OpenAI told DFD in a statement. “We need public and private sector cooperation, including pathways for companies to share threat information, improve detection and enforcement, and strengthen collective defense that build upon existing work in this space." The FTC declined to comment. OSTP, the DOJ, Anthropic and Google did not respond to inquiries.

Apple assails Canada’s data bill

Apple is raising privacy objections to a new digital records bill in Canada, POLITICO’s Mickey Djuric reports.

Bill C-22 would oblige companies like Apple and Google to provide data police could use in criminal investigations to identify who is behind email addresses, phone numbers and other digital accounts. The companies would also have to maintain a system that can fulfill such requests from authorities.

Apple claims such requirements could allow for police to secretly access financial, location and health data, and could end up forcing the company to weaken end-to-end encryption. The Canadian government has denied this, however.

The European Union will postpone restrictions on high-risk applications of AI until December 2027, POLITICO’s Pieter Haeck reports.

The provisions are a key part of the EU’s AI Act, and were set to go into effect in August. The deal reached by EU legislators Thursday also accommodates Germany’s demands for industrial AI to be regulated under a different set of rules.

The postponement marks the first major rollback of the EU’s digital rules, and follows pressure from the U.S. over its own tech laws as industry warns such restrictions could hurt Europe’s competitiveness in the global AI race. item.description: 5 Questions for Russell Wald
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

Russell Wald | Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence handout.

Russell Wald is the executive director of the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence, an organization dedicated to advancing AI research and policy that focuses on the technology’s impact on people. HAI recently published its annual Artificial Intelligence Index Report, which Wald helped to oversee. This year’s evaluation found that China has almost caught up with the U.S. in terms of the capabilities of its models. Wald talks to us about the AI competition between the U.S. and China, and the advent of “world models” that predict what might happen in real-world environments. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 

What’s one underrated big idea?

World models and their impact on governance. Spatial intelligence will fundamentally transform how we live, work and operate in the physical space. Few are aware of its looming implications, but it is coming, and we need to be prepared for it.

It will require a different form of governance than [for] LLMs. There will be different areas related to privacy, related to the effect on jobs.

What’s a technology that you think is overhyped?

Humanoid robots in the near term. The long-term potential could be significant, but there is a tendency to just conflate the impressive demonstrations with broad economic readiness.

What could the government be doing regarding technology that it isn’t?

Deeply funding academia much more than it is. The Genesis Mission is a great start, but we need to do much more in this space. And in particular, we need to really have a much more robust national AI research resource. This is really important and can lead to a greater open source community, and allow us to build on top of each other much more effectively than we are right now.

The Create AI Act [for a national AI research resource] … would be a great start. There was interest in the Biden administration. There's interest in the Trump administration. There's interest in Congress. I think it's just more about really understanding what the impact will be and to double down on it.

What book most shaped your conception of the future?

I'm going to go back to a book that I read in high school, but still affects me: “Hiroshima” by John Hersey. That has a profound effect on me because the horror described in the book comes down to decision makers, and what decision-makers can do with the power that they have. I'm not judging right or wrong the decision [to drop the nuclear bomb]. What I am saying is the impacts of that decision have reverberations for the world to this very day.

Decision-makers have a unique responsibility with what they do and how they do it. Their enormous decisions might be made behind a desk, but those decisions affect generations.

What has surprised you the most this year?

It's not an apples-to-apples comparison, but despite the fact that the U.S. has about $285 billion in private investment in AI, and China has a little over $12 billion, [China] has still been able to close the model performance gap with the U.S.

Some people are claiming distillation [a method of extracting an AI model’s capabilities] is what's gotten China there. I think one of the biggest stories, though, is the robust open-source ecosystem that the Chinese have. They have just deeply invested in their talent base, and have diffused the technology broadly.

Senior administration officials are trying to allay concerns about the prospect of requiring pre-approvals for the release of frontier AI models, POLITICO reports.

That suggestion sparked concerns among tech executives and industry-aligned policy groups.

Soon after Hassett’s statement, White House chief of staff Susie Wiles wrote in a rare X post that the administration is “not in the business of picking winners and losers.” A senior White House official also told POLITICO that Hassett's remarks were “taken out of context a little bit” and that the White House is looking for “partnership” with companies rather than pursuing “government regulation.”

Twelve Democratic senators sent a letter on Thursday urging the Federal Communications Commission to cease its early review of Disney’s broadcast licenses, POLITICO’s John Hendel reports.

FTC Chair Brendan Carr issued an order late last month to review Disney’s licenses for eight of its ABC broadcast TV stations years before it was scheduled. item.title: America’s gamble on satellite broadband gets real
item.description: America’s gamble on satellite broadband gets real
item.content:encoded:
Presented by Association for Competitive Technology: How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By John Hendel

Presented by 

With help from Aaron Mak

SpaceX is set to get a massive amount of funding under a broadband expansion program. | Mario Tama/Getty Images

America is about to make a big bet on high-speed satellite internet that promises a new model for how space technology could digitally connect the most remote parts of the country — assuming it works.

Clusters of low-Earth orbit satellites have provided internet access to soldiers on the front lines in Ukraine, to protesters during Iran’s recent internet blackout, and following natural disasters. But the technology is relatively new and unproven, even as it promises to bring high-speed internet to rural and isolated parts of America at a fraction of the cost of laying down fiber cables.

The results of connecting rural America could shape the legacy of President Donald Trump, who inherited a directive from the 2021 infrastructure law to ensure all Americans can get online — an ambition frequently compared to rural electrification of the 20th century.

The nascent industry under Trump is now poised to receive a bigger chunk of a $42.45 billion broadband expansion program than it would have under former President Joe Biden. Elon Musk’s SpaceX and Jeff Bezos’s Amazon Leo are reportedly slated to receive a combined $1 billion, promising to reach more than a fifth of communities that currently lack access to high-speed internet (that's in line with current federal projections, per the National Telecommunications and Information Administration). But some broadband advocates, who have long worried SpaceX is too expensive and unreliable, want to ensure the companies can deliver — especially in remote areas with no alternatives.

“These are going to become the monopoly providers,” Nat Purser, senior policy advocate at consumer advocacy group Public Knowledge, told DFD. “I do think that it will be really critical to have consistent oversight over the next couple of years to make sure these networks are actually being used, that people can afford them and also that they're performing well.”

While the mammoth broadband program is meant to connect rural (and typically more conservative-leaning) communities, some observers question whether satellite will catch people’s attention the way fiber-optic expansion has — Starlink is already widely available nationwide, after all.

“There's no ribbon cutting,” Drew Garner, director of policy engagement for the Benton Institute for Broadband & Society, told DFD. “This is a program that was going to benefit a lot of red areas.”
 

POLITICO Security Summit

On May 12, POLITICO's Security Summit will convene administration officials, policymakers and industry leaders for urgent conversations on the most pressing issues in defense and cybersecurity – including global defense cooperation, intelligence sharing, investments in new weapons systems, defense tech, and more. Register to attend.

 
 

There were also questions this year about whether the companies would participate without major government concessions.

In January, SpaceX balked at being subjected to the same performance assessments and audits as those undertaken by other internet providers receiving government funding through the program known as the Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment program, or BEAD. SpaceX even tried to get states to drop many requirements, threatening that it would be “untenable” for satellite companies to face the same standards. The attempt drew a rebuke from Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who accused the company of bullying the states.

Amazon, meanwhile, has yet to launch its retail service. In January, it asked federal regulators for a two-year extension to meet its July 30 license deadline for launching 1,618 satellites over struggles to schedule launches (The company had more than 300 satellites in orbit by April).

The National Telecommunications and Information Administration, which oversees the BEAD program, is confident that the companies vetted by the states “will get the job done,” according to a spokesperson, who added the government will use random performance testing to ensure compliance with the program’s rules, which include speed and reliability metrics. 

“NTIA can seek to suspend or claw back funding from any subgrantee that fails to meet program requirements,” the spokesperson added.

Despite some skepticism and uncertainty, some in Washington say the technology is poised to save taxpayers money while getting the same outcome for rural communities.

“Why don’t you just use satellite internet service?” Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) asked Lutnick during a February hearing. “For $600 bucks you can buy a Starlink terminal — why don’t you just do that and do that across America and save a bunch of money?”

As time passes, the satellite companies are also fine-tuning their offerings in a bid to sway skeptics. Musk recently slashed promotional prices and showcased higher speeds his satellites can achieve. Starlink recently surpassed 10 million global subscribers. Amazon funds a year-old coalition devoted to promoting the merits of low Earth orbit satellite connectivity.

Still, not everyone is sure the tradeoffs will be worth it.

Early last year, one former federal official worried that the administration would wind up “stranding all or part of rural America with worse internet.” Skeptics like Benton’s Garner believe satellites will fall short of the fast, reliable connectivity many businesses need. And while government aid may offset the cost of installing terminals in households, he worries consumers may have to foot the bill for slashing adjacent foliage so satellite signals can clearly reach homes (SpaceX contends Starlink is getting better at routing around obstacles like trees and buildings).

In certain rugged states like Montana and Colorado, satellite companies won bids to connect at least half of their underserved locations. One Coloradan who’s run a traditional telecom network for decades worries what will happen as consumers and businesses demand higher speeds over time.

“It just seems like, look at all this money, we're going to use it, and there's no forethought,” Brian Creveling, general manager of Bijou Telephone Co-op and president of the Colorado Telecommunications Association, told DFD. “Are we going to have to give the satellite providers an insane amount of money to keep upgrading their networks as well? So I don't know. The future is uncertain.”

AI developed a zero-day exploit

Google announced that it has found evidence for the first time that hackers used AI to develop a zero-day exploit, POLITICO’s Maggie Miller reports.

In a report released Monday, the Google Threat Intelligence Group said the hackers planned to use the vulnerability for a “mass exploitation event.” The company alerted the firm affected by the vulnerability, which was patched before the announcement. The disclosure comes as the Trump administration races to establish safeguards against cyber threats posed by powerful models like Mythos. Google concluded that Mythos likely wasn’t used to create this particular exploit.

“For every zero-day we can trace back to AI, there are probably many more out there,” said GTIG chief analyst John Hultquist. “Threat actors are using AI to boost the speed, scale, and sophistication of their attacks.”
 

A message from Association for Competitive Technology:
 
GM hit with $12.75M privacy fine

California authorities announced Friday that General Motors will pay a $12.75 million fine for allegedly violating the state’s stringent Consumer Privacy Act, POLITICO’s Tyler Katzenberger reports.

State regulators claim the company made about $20 million from 2020 to 2024 by selling customers’ emails, location data and other personal information without consent to data brokers. Regulators say the data was collected via the OnStar safety platform, and that it was used to help set insurance rates in some cases. “We hope other companies that collect consumer data take note,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta told reporters on Friday. “If we get word that a company is illegally collecting, storing or selling consumer data, we won't hesitate to look under the hood and hold them accountable.”

GM spokesperson Lisa Suchland noted in a statement that the company discontinued the practice in 2024. “We’re committed to being clear and transparent with our customers,” she said.

item.description: What Mythos means for the China summit
item.content:encoded:
Presented by Association for Competitive Technology: How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

Presented by 

President Donald Trump is visiting Beijing this week. | Greg Baker/AFP via Getty Images

President Donald Trump’s trip to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping this week presents a new opportunity to establish guardrails to curb risks stemming from the AI race.

The Wall Street Journal first reported that the Trump administration has considered using the visit to start a formal dialogue between the countries to mitigate the risks posed by artificial intelligence. Potential subjects of discussion could include runaway models and autonomous weapons, according to the report. A White House official later told DFD that Trump is planning to discuss AI during his trip.

If AI safety talks do end up on the agenda, the U.S. has a major advantage: Anthropic’s Mythos model. According to the company, Mythos can exploit previously unknown vulnerabilities in a variety of operating systems and web browsers. The New York Times reported that a Chinese think tank has already requested access to Mythos, which was denied.

So, assuming the U.S. comes from a position of strength, how should it approach such dialogue, and what could realistically be achieved? Some foreign policy analysts told DFD that Mythos could help convince China to get on board with AI safety standards down the line, but short-term expectations should be low.

“China is only going to see this as a matter of power and leverage in national security,” said Hudson Institute senior fellow Bill Drexel, who studies AI competition with China. “They may project that they see [AI dialogue] as goodwill, but we should be very skeptical of that.”

Negotiating with China on issues like nuclear weapons or Covid-19 generally hasn’t worked out all that well in the past. According to Drexel, Beijing has a history of flouting international pacts it has previously agreed to. The threat of Mythos could eventually strongarm China into making meaningful concessions, but old habits die hard and advancing AI is a main priority for the country.

“Given the Mythos asymmetry [China] is now facing … it's in our interest to pressure them to institute more safety [standards] around their own releases of models for cyber- and bio-security,” said Drexel. “What's most politically feasible [for the summit] is a generic goodwill statement of mutual understanding with no teeth that sends good vibes.”

Drexel and Council on Foreign Relations senior fellow Chris McGuire, who worked on China tech competition as a deputy senior director at the Biden administration’s National Security Council, told DFD that the U.S. should focus on widening its lead with Mythos and other powerful models. The further the U.S. gets ahead of China, the more productive the dialogue will become. Yet, they both said this isn’t necessarily an argument for backing away from AI regulations to allow for innovation at breakneck speed.

“China is going to have a Mythos-level model in eight months … so we just have to make sure that we're expanding that lead,” said McGuire. He added that once the U.S. pulls far enough ahead, then it can use the dialogues to more effectively push China to institute AI safety policies that are similar to ours.

“Having strong controls and a big lead over China actually enables you to have more flexibility and autonomy on the domestic regulatory side to develop the policies that you … actually think are best,” McGuire told DFD. “Then you can push those on the China side.” Those regulations could include red lines for ethical AI use and restrictions on access to models that are capable of developing nuclear or bio weapons.

However, it’s possible that the summit will give the U.S. a chance to question the idea that it is locked in a race with China to develop something even more consequential than Mythos, like artificial general intelligence.

“There's very little evidence at all that China is racing towards AGI,” said Yi-Ling Liu, a China tech journalist and commentator. “There's very little evidence that China even sees AI in the same way that the U.S. does in terms of this kind of omnipotent technology that will guarantee an irreversible victory.” According to Liu, communications for the Chinese government suggest that it sees AI as being more akin to a technology like electricity that should augment the economy, rather than as a nuclear weapon that it has to race to build.

If the dialogue leads to that kind of understanding, then the race framework won’t be as much of an obstacle to cooperating on AGI and other forms of the technology, Liu added.

“We have to just step back and think about: What exactly is the race, and what does racing even mean?” she told DFD. “It is possible to remain competitive, [and to] introduce technologies to different sectors of society without completely letting go of regulation and institutional oversight.”

“President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump will have an in-depth exchange of views on major issues concerning China-U.S. relations and world peace and development,” said China’s U.S. embassy spokesperson Liu Pengyu, who declined to comment specifically on AI. Anthropic did not respond to an inquiry.

Rep. Frank Pallone has opened an investigation into how companies calculate individualized prices using personal data, POLITICO’s Alfred Ng exclusively reports.

Pallone, who is the ranking Democrat on the House Energy and Commerce Committee, sent letters to Amazon, Walmart and 23 other companies inquiring into matters such as how they collect people’s info and whether they disclose their surveillance pricing practices to their customers.

Reps. Chris Deluzio (D-Penn.) and Erin Houchin (R-Ind.) introduced a bill on Tuesday to create age-based screentime recommendations, the details of which POLITICO’s Gabby Miller was the first to report.
