item.description: The plaintiffs’ attorney taking on social media giants
item.content:encoded:
Presented by Association for Competitive Technology: How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Hassan Ali Kanu

Presented by 

With help from Aaron Mak

Social Media Victims Law Center founder Matthew Bergman talks to DFD about the kids safety lawsuits against Meta. | Tony Avelar/AP

Matthew Bergman, founder of the Social Media Victims Law Center, has helped lead some of the first lawsuits seeking to hold tech giants liable for harms allegedly caused by social media platforms. As major cases against Meta and YouTube advance — including a New Mexico trial in which a judge is currently considering a range of penalties to be imposed on Meta — Bergman spoke with DFD about the growing product liability push against Big Tech and how companies are responding.

Are you working with the states and the school districts who are alleging much the same claims as in your cases? 

There are two other types of cases pending in the multi-district litigation. One is cases of school districts seeking essentially compensation for the enhanced mental health services they have to provide based on [the alleged harms caused by social media]. And the other is attorneys general acting on their police powers to bring consumer-based cases against these companies.

My firm specifically is not actively involved in the trials, but we are very collaborative with attorneys general around the country. As the plaintiffs bar we are actively engaged with them, we are sharing expert witnesses, and in many cases we are assisting in trial presentation.

What are your thoughts on the proceedings thus far in the New Mexico v. Meta remedies trial? 

I’ve tried enough cases that I've given up predicting, I find I jinx it if I do that. The fact that they are in a trial the way they are is a good thing. That’s an important point: When we started no one thought we’d ever get past a motion to dismiss, let alone summary judgement, let alone a trial before a jury. The fact that these cases are being tried is testimony to the hard work and incredible acumen of the [litigators]. We’re not gonna win every case — it doesn’t work that way — and we don’t have to.

With respect to how it’ll impact the broader field: The more opportunities plaintiffs — be they government entities or injured individuals — have to present to a fair and impartial jury the more pressure these companies will face to implement changes they know they need to in order to make the platforms less pernicious.

Facebook has argued in part that other social media companies do not use the kinds of safeguards they may be ordered to implement, and that people can find ways around certain safety protocols. What do you make of those arguments, and how they may land with New Mexico Judge Bryan Biedscheid?

To some extent, that argument is that “we’ll lose money.” If I build a car and put airbags on it I guess I would be at a competitive disadvantage to a company that doesn’t put airbags on a car. So what? That’s your problem. I don’t think those are viable arguments.

Regarding workarounds, well you can disable an airbag. You can take the catalytic converter out of your car. Inevitably there are workarounds, particularly when dealing with kids who are ingenious, it’s an iterative process to make changes, and they’re not gonna be perfect. So what? Let's not let the perfect be the enemy of the good. I find those arguments fatuous.

Meta has threatened that it may have to leave New Mexico due to the court-ordered remedies. What are your thoughts there?

Make my day. I think it’s probably true that New Mexico is a small enough state that they could do that, I guess that’s [an option]. But so what? Honestly, if you can't make the product safe then don’t sell it.

You don’t seem concerned that the prospect of losing access to Facebook or Instagram could turn the public relations fight in Meta’s favor. Why not?

I’ve talked to too many parents who have lost kids. And in the context of product liability we have this concept called “risk utility,” and it basically means that you look at a particular product and you weigh the risks and benefits. So if you have a cancer drug that works, that 9 out of 10 times cures a person, and one time it makes it worse, society would probably say that’s a product worth having because there’s a risk but the utility is so great.

With respect to social media: If the risk is kids dying and the utility is you get to hook up with your old college girlfriend on the internet … I don’t think the social good, under anybody’s scenario, is so great that we should accept the level of carnage we’re seeing in our young people. Can [we] look around now that we are in a social media world and say we’re that much better than 20 years ago before we had it?

China hawks become doves

Republican China hawks have been conspicuously silent in the run-up to President Donald Trump’s visit to Beijing, POLITICO’s Jack Detsch, Katherine Long and Paul McLeary report.

The lack of vocal warnings about the Chinese Communist Party as Trump prepares to strike new deals on tech and trade suggests an overall softening of Washington’s posture toward Beijing. The president has approved sales of Nvidia’s H200 chips to China and allowed TikTok to continue operating in the U.S., which have previously raised alarm from national security-focused lawmakers. He told reporters he plans to talk about arms sales to Taiwan with Chinese President Xi Jinping, a departure from longstanding U.S. policy to avoid consulting with Beijing on the subject.

Trump is also bringing Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang along, sparking speculation there could be negotiations over chips. Sen. Steve Daines (R-Mont.) said he was “thrilled” about Huang’s attendance, adding that the CEO is “one of the greatest thought leaders” when it comes to chips. Sen. Meta is providing competing AI chatbots with free access to WhatsApp for a month as it tries to work out an antitrust settlement with European Union regulators, POLITICO’s Jacob Parry reports.

The European Commission launched an antitrust investigation into Meta in December after the company instituted a policy that prohibited third-party chatbots from communicating with users via WhatsApp’s business interface. item.title: AI cyber fears get a reality check
item.description: AI cyber fears get a reality check
item.content:encoded:
Presented by Association for Competitive Technology: How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

Presented by 

Anthropic's Claude Mythos Preview model has caused concern in D.C. | Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images

Washington has been in a heightened state of concern in the five weeks since Anthropic announced the creation of Mythos.

Mythos’ purported ability to exploit previously unknown software vulnerabilities has spurred the administration to hurriedly convene meetings with industry at the White House, devise a potential executive order on AI cyber threats and use the model to secure government systems.

Yet administration officials and tech industry executives who spoke at the Risk Operations Conference in Virginia Thursday didn’t seem all that spooked. In fact, the overall message seemed to be: Take a breath. There was a general consensus that AI will rapidly augment cyber defense, and attackers aren’t likely to get the upper hand.

Daniel Richard, an associate deputy director at the Central Intelligence Agency, even said he was “quite bullish” about what AI means for cybersecurity.

“This isn’t transactional,” Richard told the audience in a rare public appearance from a CIA official. “This is us as a country figuring out with the academic community, with the private sector community, with our public sector partners [how to] take advantage of what I see as an optimal opportunity for the agency.”

Moving quickly to integrate AI-enabled cyber defenses into government systems, and to develop new standards for the technology, was a major theme of the discussions. “[In] this administration, the priority is speed,” said Victoria Yan Pillitteri, a supervisory computer scientist at the National Institute of Standards and Technology.

By that same token, officials and executives talked up how AI will streamline cyber operations. “We cannot control how the attackers are ... trying to exploit things, [but] what we can control is how fast we can respond,” said Sumedh Thakar, CEO of the cybersecurity company Qualys, which put on the conference. “[If] we can use AI to automate and get to the point where we can patch and fix things in a matter of two to three hours, then we don't have to worry too much.”

Qualys currently has access to OpenAI’s GPT‑5.5 Cyber and has been using it to help secure systems in both private industry and the public sector. Based on that work so far, Thakar said that most sensitive government systems should be secure against these models within months, and there will be more widespread resilience efforts in the next few years.

There are other AI applications that should go a long way to helping cyber defenders, too. Richard noted that the CIA has begun using AI agents to help cybersecurity personnel make recommendations and triage their work. “There will be a critical recalibration of what our officers are going to be required to do [with] human-machine teaming,” he said.

Pillitteri cautioned, though, that more guidelines are needed for AI integration into government cyber operations. “How do we secure that AI? How do we ensure that those AI systems, those AI agents are trustworthy?” she said, adding: “A really foundational part of this conversation ... is often overlooked when we're excited about leveraging [AI], and this is, of course, standards.”

The event’s generally calm tone may reflect a growing familiarity with systems like Mythos and GPT‑5.5 Cyber. “Maybe the first couple of weeks [after the Mythos announcement] people were a lot more like, ‘Oh my God,’” Thakar told DFD. “And then that conversation moved towards, ‘Okay, well it's here — how do we focus on making sure we are doing the right thing to defend ourselves?'”

The CMA is still determining whether Microsoft's Copilot AI app will be included in the investigation.

“Our aim is to understand how these markets are developing, Microsoft’s position within them and to consider what, if any, targeted action may be needed to ensure U.K. organizations can benefit from choice, innovation and competitive prices,” said CMA chief executive Sarah Cardell in a statement.

A Microsoft spokesperson said, “We are committed to working quickly and constructively with the CMA to facilitate its review of the business software market.”

A new poll indicates that Americans don’t know a lot about AI companies, but are generally skeptical of the industry, POLITICO’s Calder McHugh reports.

A 1,078-person survey conducted by the political consultancy Slingshot Strategies found most respondents didn’t have many opinions about particular AI companies because they don’t know enough to differentiate them. They broadly expressed suspicion about how ethical the industry’s conduct is, and only 15 percent indicated that using AI in war is necessary or inevitable.

“AI being used in war just seems like a cowardly tactic,” said a 29-year-old Missouri Republican. “People that don’t have enough guts to fight on their own terms — it really states a huge decline in this country’s moral fabric.”

item.title: 5 Questions for Jonathan Siddharth
item.description: 5 Questions for Jonathan Siddharth
item.content:encoded:
Presented by Association for Competitive Technology: How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

Presented by 

With help from Hassan Ali Kanu

Jonathan Siddharth | Turing handout.

Jonathan Siddharth is the co-founder and CEO of Turing, a company focused on accelerating progress toward artificial general intelligence. Turing provides code, data and digital infrastructure for top AI developers like Google and Anthropic, and OpenAI personally consulted Siddharth as it was developing ChatGPT. Siddharth talks to us about the importance of humans in generating data for models, and how the education system should change to adapt to the advent of AI. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 

What’s one underrated big idea?

The importance of improving frontier models from real-world [deployment] data. If you look at how all these models are trained, a lot of it is two types of data. One is data for pre-training — you train the models on the internet or other existing sources of knowledge, like books. And then there's post-training, where typically the recipe is you hire experts who are generating data for supervised fine-tuning or building environments for reinforcement learning.

The underrated idea is how much you learn from actual deployments. When you actually use some of the frontier models to automate real workflows — let's say in financial services or asset management — you discover where things actually break. You can use that to advance the models.

What’s a technology you think is overhyped?

The use of pure synthetic data. When you generate data to improve the models in coding, oftentimes the workflow is hybrid, where maybe there is a large language model generating [version one] of the data, humans improving it and LLMs helping humans keep quality high. It's sort of humans and AI working together to generate data. That is super helpful. And of course, when you build a reinforcement learning environment, there is some level of synthetic data that is being generated when the agent is trying … to figure out which trajectories result in a reward versus not.

Some people think of synthetic data as purely a bigger model for teaching a smaller model. That works when you are training a student model with a teacher model, but pure synthetic data is not super helpful when you want to advance the teacher model itself. Pure synthetic data may be somewhat overhyped in the general public. I think researchers know that the best data pipeline is a hybrid of human and AI/synthetic data.

What could the government be doing regarding technology that it isn’t?

We need to be thinking really carefully about how we mitigate the impact of job displacement, and rethink education. How do we change the education system in a world where superintelligence exists?

I would teach math, computer science and AI very, very early. It's important for people to understand how these models are trained. That's foundational to using them in ways that are economically valuable.

Humans are very specialized by and large. There's somebody who specializes in software engineering, somebody who specializes in finance. Human capacity for learning is at a certain level, but in a world where you have superintelligence, all of us can be much more multidimensional. Teaching people to be more generalist problem solvers with access to these powerful tools will be important. I feel like the output of the educational system today is relatively more specialized, with people getting into these different professions. I think in the future it could be the case that it's a lot broader.

What book most shaped your conception of the future?

Elon Musk by Walter Isaacson. The thing I appreciated in how [Musk] built his companies was the level of urgency and him being able to do what he did across so many very different industries — whether it's SpaceX, Tesla, xAI, Neuralink, PayPal. It expanded my sense of what a single human can accomplish if you operate a certain way.

What has surprised you the most this year?

How quickly these [AI] agents have mastered building software and general computer use to do all types of knowledge work. I feel like these models are going to accelerate human productivity in very significant ways. I think the way to experience it is just by building with it yourself directly. The thing with exponential curves is that it’s very hard for humans to understand. You're constantly reminded of how magical it is when it happens.

The Trump administration is considering intervening in a lawsuit alleging that Elon Musk’s xAI is illegally operating more than two dozen polluting gas turbines to power a massive data center in Mississippi for its Grok chatbot.

The NAACP sued xAI and subsidiary MZX Tech in April, claiming the companies violated the Clean Air Act by operating the turbines without necessary permits or mandatory pollution controls. item.title: Silicon Valley wants inside your head
item.description: Silicon Valley wants inside your head
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Calder McHugh

With help from Aaron Mak

Brain-computer interface systems are at the center of a policy debate. | Kevin Frayer/Getty Images

It’s inevitable. Eventually, according to one of Silicon Valley’s most well-connected venture capitalists, we’ll all submit to implanting a Neuralink-style chip in our brains.

“Someone you work with will get it first. And you’ll hold out for a while, the way you did with the smartphone. But eventually, you won’t,” D. Scott Phoenix, who founded the neurotechnology company Vicarious before moving into investing, said at TED 2026 in Vancouver last month, dressed in all black with a tiny mic attached to his ear. “The advantages of integration will be hard to compete with.”

Put bluntly, in his view, “We’re on the cusp of the next major transition, the merger of humans and AI.”

The transhumanist vision is no longer confined to the fringes of Silicon Valley. Digitally enhanced cognition, once dismissed as science fiction, is increasingly becoming both a serious business proposition and a live policy debate, as advocates for neural privacy try to beef up industry regulation.

Phoenix is not the only one in Silicon Valley who believes this. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman mused way back in 2017 that “a merge is probably our best-case scenario” for survival after the emergence of superhuman AI.

And behind all this talk about rewiring humanity itself is a fast-growing industry. Huge sums of money are pouring into technology designed to blur the boundary between human cognition and machines. The broader neurotechnology market is projected to expand to $55 billion by 2032, according to the Neurorights Foundation.

Thus far, the use case for implantable devices is largely medical. Noland Arbaugh, the first human to receive a brain-computer interface from the Musk-founded Neuralink, is paralyzed from the neck down but is now able to use a computer with his mind. As of January, Neuralink has reported 21 human clinical trials, following years of controversial primate testing.

There are also less intrusive forms of BCI. Wearable technology like smart glasses, fitness wristbands or stress-tracking apps are already widespread. These products are lucrative for manufacturers not just because millions of consumers buy them, but because of what companies can extract in return: neural data.

And as the industry grows, a nascent political movement is forming, aimed at protecting consumers’ brain data.

In Colorado, California and Connecticut, legislators have amended existing privacy statutes to include information that is generated by a “consumer’s central or peripheral nervous system.” Montana has gone further, requiring consent, access, deletion and destruction obligations around any neural data. And Minnesota is in the midst of considering a broad “neurodata rights” framework that goes beyond an expansion of privacy protections.

At the federal level, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, along with Sens. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) and Ed Markey (D-Mass.), introduced the MIND Act last September. The bill would direct the Federal Trade Commission to study how neural data can reveal thoughts, emotions, or decision-making patterns — and how it and related data should be regulated.

Many of these proposals have been written in part by the Neurorights Foundation, a global advocacy group that reports funding from the Omidyar Network and the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation. The foundation says it is now working to expand to nine other states laws enacted in California, Colorado, Montana and Connecticut.

“Neurotechnologies have wonderful and profound implications to enhance human flourishing,” said Stephen Damianos, the CEO of the Neurorights Foundation. “Without common sense regulations and safeguards, there is risk that humanity will never benefit from what these technologies have to offer.”

That approach, and in particular a focus on state-level legislation, has alarmed company leaders.

“For innovation to happen in this space, we can’t be navigating 50 different legislative agendas,” said Ryan Field, the CEO of the neurotechnology company Kernel. “Let’s get the right stakeholders involved, so that you have actual subject matter experts and not just science fiction enthusiasts writing laws.”

According to some of Silicon Valley’s leading evangelists, it’s only a matter of time before chips are implanted in all of our brains. Perhaps they are fooling themselves, or perhaps they just see a chance to make a lot of money. But for many, this is their honest conviction.

For advocates and others concerned about privacy, no matter what the future looks like, it shouldn’t solely be determined by tech companies with a profit motive. Such political backlash could endanger the very dreams of those hoping to build a new world.

“Transhumanists that I know are very worried that their well-intentioned views on human flourishing could instead not be realized because of technosurveillance and human rights abuses,” said Susan Schneider, the director of the Center for the Future of AI, Mind and Society at Florida Atlantic University.
Head of U.S. AI cyber effort under criticism

Trump administration officials and tech industry representatives are worried that National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross is not equipped to lead the White House’s response to rapidly advancing artificial intelligence models with potentially dangerous hacking capabilities, POLITICO reports.

Four current U.S. officials and five industry representatives told POLITICO they fear Cairncross, who has little previous cybersecurity experience, is not acting with the urgency and technical expertise required to address Mythos and similarly powerful models. According to people familiar with the exchange, JP Morgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon went to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent with concerns about the speed and coordination of the government’s AI cybersecurity efforts. Some in the industry are also disgruntled by the lack of federal guidance on the threat, and by efforts to fast-track an executive order on the matter before receiving more input.

White House Spokesperson Liz Huston wrote in a statement, “Sean Cairncross is doing excellent work to protect the American people and our nation’s critical infrastructure from cyber threats, working closely with senior administration officials and American companies to advance shared objectives and priorities — including addressing cybersecurity challenges posed by the rapid scaling of artificial intelligence — while continuing President Trump’s commitment to ensuring American technological dominance.”

JP Morgan Chase spokesperson Trish Wexler said the company appreciates “the leadership of the Administration and the White House on this complex, evolving issue and their continued engagement with critical infrastructure.”

The Treasury Department declined to comment, and Cairncross’ office did not respond to inquiries.
Jury dismisses Musk’s OpenAI suit

A federal jury in California dismissed Elon Musk’s lawsuit alleging that OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman deceived him into funding the company with the understanding that it would remain as a nonprofit, POLITICO’s Hassan Ali Kanu reports.

The unanimous jury decided in just a few hours on Monday that Musk’s allegations of unjust enrichment and breach of charitable trust were past the statute of limitations. The jurors made the same finding concerning a related claim that Microsoft had aided and abetted that breach.

District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers, who had been administering a parallel proceeding about potential remedies on Monday, announced that she would accept the non-binding advisory verdict. Musk had sought remedies including over $100 billion in damages, restructuring of OpenAI back into a nonprofit and removal of Altman as an executive. Musk is expected to appeal.

item.description: The politics of owning a tech company
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

The Hustle app supported Sen. Bernie Sanders’ (I-Vt.) 2016 presidential campaign. | Brett Carlsen/Getty Images

Hustle is a popular app among Democratic campaigns for sending personalized messages encouraging recipients to vote and organize. Hustle first rose to prominence by supporting grassroots outreach for Sen. Bernie Sanders’ (I-Vt.) 2016 presidential bid, and has since worked with campaigns for Sens. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) and Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.). Despite working with progressive candidates, Hustle has been owned by prominent tech entrepreneur Chamath Palihapitiya’s venture capital firm Social Capital since 2020. Palihapitiya, a co-host of the popular All-In podcast, became a well-known supporter of President Donald Trump during the 2024 election. 

Hustle announced today that Social Capital has sold the company to its employees, who hope that the new ownership structure will better fit their values. Palihapitiya told DFD in an email, “I sold Hustle to them to harvest capital losses to net against some other gains. I initiated the transaction on my own volition. That said, I wish them the best of luck.”

DFD spoke to Hustle CEO Jesse Hassinger about what led up to the sale, and what it means for a tech company to be owned by its employees. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 

What was the issue with Hustle’s previous ownership? 

Unfortunately, in 2024, what we encountered was Chamath’s decision to support Trump in the election. There was now a misalignment between the values of customers, and the values of leaders and ownership of the company. Though the day-to-day operations did not change ... that was very difficult on a human level for employees of the company. You can imagine dedicating yourself to a cause or a mission, and [then] you learn that your boss is dedicating his time and energy to causes that are in competition with the vision that you're trying to see in the world.

Coming out of 2024, it was a hard year for customers and employees who were sticking with it. Some trust was lost in that period of time, understandably.

What makes this ownership structure unusual in the tech industry?

It's a very rare win for employees. Employees are not having a good year. [The structure] is unusual in a lot of dimensions. Going from VC ownership to employee ownership — that's unusual.

How we've organized governance as well as financial ownership of Hustle is also really different. For a typical VC-funded organization, as a new employee, the ratio of distribution of equity between you and a leader might be like 500 to one. We've essentially made sure that even for the most recent employee, that ratio is like four to one. When there's a vote that requires participation from the owners of the company, employees will be able to cast a vote and make decisions that determine the direction of the company.

Why is it that campaign tech companies tend to only work with one political party or the other, along partisan lines?

It's about trust — trust with data, trust with support and services. Partisanship is at all-time highs, so we see in this particular space [that] there is a bifurcation between tools that support one set of causes or the other, and they generally fall along partisan lines. This is not typical in other marketplaces, but [trust] is very important in civic tech. There are tools that work with all sides — they tend to be used less often because of that trust principle.

I would’ve thought working with only one party would limit your business. But working with both parties limits it even more? 

If you're working for all sides, it's definitely a choice. In my experience and from conversations, picking a side is an important decision that a business will make when operating in this particular space. One of our first customers was Bernie Sanders, texting college kids that if they were feeling the Bern, they should head to the stadium. That's where we got our start, so we made our choice a long time ago.

There’s a growing divide between the political values of tech company executives and their employees. What do you think is driving that divide?

The social contract between employers and employees has been somewhat frayed, which we're seeing increasingly in software engineering and technology. These were jobs that were not just coveted, but were also highly rewarded and incentivized for commitment to those tech companies. There's anxiety and precariousness around longevity in those careers, and there's been an incredible number of layoffs. Just at a very human level, being dislocated from a job you might have had for 20 years at an organization that's printing beaucoup bucks — it’s heartbreaking.

The pendulum has swung very fast in one direction that favors some of these larger corporate entities. Employees will find it hard to have their voices heard by the leaders of those companies. That is where organized labor traditionally has come in. The role of labor in this new environment will become more relevant. I suspect that will become a new opportunity for employees to organize their workspaces.
A bipartisan bill for circuit boards

Sens. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) and Jim Justice (R-W.Va.) introduced a bill on Tuesday to incentivize domestic printed circuit board manufacturing, DFD has exclusively learned.

The Protecting Circuit Boards and Substrates Act would provide a 25 percent tax credit for purchasing or acquiring American-made PCBs — which are the thin green panels that act as the connective tissue for a device's semiconductors. U.S. global market share for PCBs has dropped from 30 percent over the past few decades to four percent, making Silicon Valley dependent on imports from China. The global PCB supply chain has also been strained by the Iran war.

DFD previously reported that the dearth of domestic PCB manufacturing could be a major bottleneck as the U.S. moves to integrate AI into robotics. PCBs typically need to be custom-designed for a particular robot model, and companies often incur tariffs every time they make modifications.

“Arizona is emerging as a key leader in semiconductor manufacturing. But those chips are useless without the printed circuit boards that make them work,” Gallego said in a statement.

Justice said, “America must do everything we can to stay competitive with other countries around the world, and that starts with making more products right here at home — including printing circuit boards.”
UK science minister struggles with AI adoption

The United Kingdom’s minister for science, innovation, research and nuclear said during a Monday conference that it has been “unbelievably difficult” and a “painful first-hand experience” to get his office to use AI, POLITICO’s Frank Hersey reports.

At the Institute for the Future of Work conference, Patrick Vallance said he had told his staff early in his tenure, “Let’s be the office that uses AI to try and get as much done as we can.” He added, though, that “it has been unbelievably difficult to get that going.” While Vallance stated that he has a “great person” working on the effort, the “challenge of then embedding that properly in the way the place works has given me a painful first-hand experience of what this really looks like.”

According to the minister, the experience has helped him to understand how difficult AI adoption may be in workplaces “even if you can see the obvious benefits of it.” Yet he still appears hopeful about the effort, noting: “None of that is a reason not to get on with it fast.”

item.title: The new race to keep up with AI
item.description: The new race to keep up with AI
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

Anthropic recently reported that its AI is showing early signs of recursive self-improvement. | Don Feria/AP

In what could be the first step toward the AI apocalypse — or a techutopia, depending on who you ask — the technology is purportedly on the precipice of autonomously improving itself without human intervention.

Taken to the extreme, recursive self-improvement, or RSI, could lead to artificial intelligence that autonomously advances to the point at which humans are no longer able to control it — a theoretical milestone known as the singularity. That could cause the technology to wipe out humanity, or usher in the kind of leisurely world without work that Elon Musk has envisioned. There are plenty of less dramatic outcomes for RSI, though, which may arguably be more likely. In any case, it’s unclear if society is ready to handle the impact after Anthropic disclosed early signs of RSI in its AI earlier this month.

If humanity is already struggling with the technology right now, how can we hope to regulate this latest twist? Existing and proposed policies for current AI — like auditing its code, prohibiting certain uses (think nuclear weapons) or requiring government approval before releasing a model — may be inadequate if the technology is autonomously advancing faster than humans can react. Some legal and computer science researchers told DFD that RSI will force us to rethink what viable AI regulation looks like.

“When you are going into RSI, you are setting yourself up to have a system that can iterate faster than anybody can track,” said Eran Kahana, an attorney and AI research fellow at Stanford Law School. “RSI [has the] ability to self-iterate and basically become something that is unrecognizable.”

One solution could be to set up liability rules early. It’s hard to predict what harm RSI might cause, but you could imagine a scenario in which a model upgrades itself enough to evade safeguards and cause a biohazard disaster. In such an event, there would need to be a way to figure out who is responsible for any deaths and injuries.

The liability framework could take several forms.

An industry-friendly approach would be to focus on whether the developer should have reasonably foreseen the harm caused by their model. This regime addresses the fact that RSI may cause AI to evolve in unexpected ways, and a developer becomes less and less liable the more the model changes from its original state. The upside of this regime is that it would promote innovation, yet it could also make it harder for victims to get justice.

A safety-focused approach could impose strict liability, which would hold developers responsible regardless of whether they expected a model to iterate in a certain way. It’s the same standard we use for accidents at nuclear plants and for oil spills.

“Of course, then there will be the people who say [that] you can’t do that because then nobody will want to develop [RSI],” said Kahana. “Maybe, maybe not.”

Similarly, Kahana suggests that there could be a statute that automatically imposes, say, a $10 million fine if any harm occurs.

An even better vehicle might be permits. In other words, the government could require permits for companies to develop RSI, through which they agree to security measures, liability insurance and whatever audits regulators deem appropriate for RSI. A permitting system might seem onerous, but Kahana contends it could be merited in the case of RSI. “I see a permit being a very viable approach,” he told DFD. “The [higher] the risk is of an application, the more amenable it is to a permit structure.”

Perhaps the worst case scenario would be RSI causing models to keep enhancing themselves to the point that humans no longer have control, which allows the technology to set off a civilization-ending disaster. In that case, regulation becomes moot.

The bluntest tool for preventing this would be to enact a moratorium on the development of AI before RSI is achieved, a proposal that David Krueger, an assistant professor of machine learning at the University of Montreal, is pushing through his activism nonprofit Evitable.

“We're about to push the button, and if the AI isn’t already aligned enough, and if the way we’ve set it up isn’t right, then we’re going to lose control of this thing,” Krueger told DFD. “The obvious policy here is just to slam the brakes.”

Yet Yu Su, assistant professor of computer science at Ohio State University, who also serves as CEO of the AI agent company NeoCognition, is skeptical that RSI will achieve what its biggest detractors predict.

“The very important distinction between these artificial entities and the biological beings is truly innate goals, survival instincts and this whole suite of traits,” he told DFD. “These traits are necessary for some being to escape our control or bring about so-called existential risks, but currently, I don’t see any plausible way to give [those] traits to AI.”
Deepfake law goes into effect

The Federal Trade Commission is taking steps to enforce the TAKE IT DOWN Act, which went into effect on Tuesday, POLITICO’s Katherine Long reports.

The law, which President Donald Trump signed last year, outlaws the dissemination of nonconsensual intimate imagery like explicit deepfakes or revenge porn. The FTC sent letters to Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and a host of other tech companies last week to remind them about their obligations to maintain a notice and removal process for such content. Platforms have to remove the nonconsensual imagery within 48 hours of it being flagged. The FTC has also launched a website for victims to submit complaints about platforms that do not adhere to the requirements.

On Wednesday, the agency sent another set of warning letters to 12 companies that allegedly offer “nudify” tools that allegedly remove people’s clothing from pictures. The letters advise the recipients that they appear to be violating the act by not providing a takedown request process.
G7 cooperates on AI cyber risks to banks

G7 countries will prioritize the cybersecurity threats that AI and quantum computing may pose to banks, POLITICO’s Gregorio Sorgi reports.

After a two-day meeting among the countries’ finance ministers in Paris, the G7 announced in a communiqué on Tuesday that its working groups would pursue “further work on quantum related risks and preparedness of the financial sector” and undertake “additional efforts to map cybersecurity risks and opportunities related to artificial intelligence.”

The effort comes after Anthropic announced in April the creation of Mythos, a powerful model that can purportedly exploit previously unknown cybersecurity vulnerabilities. The European Union’s economy commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis told reporters on Tuesday that the U.S. will provide access to Mythos in order to evaluate the implications of AI for bank security. “The U.S. provided reassurance and outlined how to share access to Mythos wider, while keeping tight control because it’s important that the model doesn’t end up in the wrong hands,” he said.

item.title: Deepfakes are testing the limits of IP law
item.description: Deepfakes are testing the limits of IP law
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

The NO FAKES Act is aimed at combatting nonconsensual deepfakes. | Rob Lever/AFP via Getty Images

Nonconsensual deepfakes have become one of the most reviled applications of AI, and Congress is now looking to use the might of intellectual property law to keep them in check.

On Wednesday, a bipartisan group of lawmakers reintroduced the NO FAKES Act, which would essentially give all Americans an IP right to their voice and likeness. The act’s sponsors promote it not only as a way to protect artists and entertainers from having their creative output co-opted by AI, but as a safeguard for everyone else against pornographic deepfakes, fraudulent impersonation and a host of other ills.

NO FAKES would considerably expand the ambit of IP, which was originally aimed at incentivizing innovation and creativity. Using IP to also address issues like misinformation and sexual exploitation arguably brings this body of law into uncharted territory. Legal scholars told DFD that marshaling IP as an all-purpose shield against malicious deepfakes may have unintended consequences.

“The challenge posed by deepfakes is real, urgent and human, but not every human harm is an intellectual property harm,” said Georgetown IP law professor Madhavi Sunder. “Intellectual property can't be everything everywhere all at once.”

The NO FAKES Act would allow anyone to sue distributors of unauthorized deepfakes depicting them. Platforms would also have to establish notice-and-takedown systems for users to report content that contains such digital replicas.

Under the law, people could give consent for use of their deepfakes by selling licenses to their personal characteristics. That may make more sense for a musician who wants to ensure they get compensated when an AI-generated version of their voice is featured in a song, or if Matthew McConaughey wants to choose which advertisers can use the technology to make his character in “Dazed and Confused” hawk a product.

It’s less clear how selling licenses would work for people who aren’t in the arts and entertainment business, or what purpose it would serve. “If the goal of this law is to protect individual dignity … you've now created a vehicle for them to license or sell that,” Sunder told DFD. “Given power imbalances, individuals are often going to sell that right pretty cheaply and easily with a click of a button: ‘I consent.’”

Those power imbalances could produce strange results when it comes to licenses. “You could also imagine mortgage lenders or payday lenders demanding that you pledge your personality rights as part of your collateral,” said Cornell tech law professor James Grimmelmann. “That gets into bad places.”

IP law for content has generally been developed around the idea that certain limits on speech are acceptable to allow artists to control and monetize their work.

It’s unclear whether that particular tradeoff works for combatting sexual exploitation or misinformation. There’s a different balance that you might want to strike depending on the circumstances in order to avoid overly chilling speech. For instance, the Take It Down Act — a law that criminalizes the distribution of nonconsensual deepfake porn — is narrower and more targeted.

“The TAKE IT DOWN Act basically says: Here's the problem … so let's just address the problem with the remedy that we think is most effective,” Sunder told DFD.

Of course, trying to regulate deepfakes piece by piece can have its disadvantages. “Your narrower provision is less likely to intrude on protected expression and people's expressive freedom, but it can also leave gaps,” said Grimmelman. “NO FAKES is more broadly trying to anticipate all kinds of future uses.”

Yet that broader approach may also unnecessarily complicate matters if, as supporters suggest, NO FAKES is also aimed at addressing fraud and impersonation.

“If you just target passing yourself off as someone, you don't get into a lot of the details about which aspects of your persona are covered or anything like that,” Grimmelman told DFD. “If you say instead that I have a right over my identity everywhere, then you have to go through the exercise of defining every kind of conduct that's wrongful or rightful in order to explain what the scope of my rights are — and that's much harder.”
Pentagon eyes AI cyber adoption

The Pentagon’s U.S. Cyber Command is establishing a task force to accelerate the adoption of AI tools with cutting-edge hacking abilities, POLITICO’s John Sakellariadis, Maggie Miller and Jacob Wendler report.

Gen. Joshua Rudd, who leads both the National Security Agency and Cyber Command, announced the task force to staff two weeks ago, according to an internal email described by two people familiar with the effort. The email indicates the task force will examine how the Pentagon can safely deploy frontier AI models in its missions.

Spokespeople for Cyber Command, the NSA and the Pentagon did not respond to a request for comment.

Lt. Gen. Charles Moore, former deputy commander of Cyber Command, said he was “aware” of the task force, and endorsed the initiative. “The Task Force can help integrate AI across operations, training, intelligence and cyber defense while ensuring the United States maintains analytic superiority over our adversaries,” he said.
ICE looks to extract Apple data

Immigration and Customs Enforcement has signed a new contract with a digital forensics company to instruct agents on how to extract encrypted data from Apple devices such as iPhones and MacBooks, POLITICO’s Alfred Ng reports.

According to federal records released on Wednesday, ICE approved a $211,618 contract with Sumuri, a Delaware-based digital forensics company. Sumuri will provide the courses “Best Practices in Mac Forensics” and “Advanced Practices in Mac Forensics.” The contract states that the courses will help enable “thorough, complex investigations involving Apple technologies.”

Apple, ICE and Sumuri did not respond to a request for comment.

item.description: 5 Questions for Sadiq Khan
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

Programming note: We’ll be off this Monday, but will be back in your inboxes on Tuesday.

London Mayor Sadiq Khan | Lia Toby/Getty Images for BFI

London Mayor Sadiq Khan has made technology a priority for his city’s agenda. Khan has sought to better leverage data for public services, install high-tech traffic cameras to improve road safety and offer residents free training in AI skills. He is also a founding member of the Mayors AI Forum, an initiative by Bloomberg Philanthropies and Johns Hopkins University that connects mayors and developers to guide deployments of the technology. Khan discusses his concerns with social media, and how data is making London cyclists safer. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 

What’s one underrated big idea?

Cities need to be at the heart of the conversation around AI. Right now, most of the focus is on the global tech companies that are building AI, or the national governments or international bodies that are racing to regulate it. But the truth is, the impacts of AI are being felt locally — in the places where people live out their daily lives — in workplaces, hospitals, classrooms, homes and streets.

City leaders are closer to our communities and have a huge role to play in making sure that we take advantage of this new technology — to improve public services, work with employers on how best they can utilize this emerging technology and make our cities fairer, safer, greener and more prosperous — while equipping our residents with the skills they need to thrive in the age of AI. That’s what the Mayors AI Forum is about. It brings together city leaders from around the world, representing more than 100 million people, to put cities at the heart of the AI conversation and make sure we’re active pioneers, not passive recipients, of this transformative technology.

What’s a technology that you think is overhyped?

In my experience, when used thoughtfully and responsibly, technology can be a powerful tool to change cities for the better and make a real difference in people’s lives. If anything, it’s underhyped.

In London, air quality sensors have helped us to tackle air pollution, new zero-emission buses are reducing our city’s carbon footprint, and high-speed 4G and 5G internet on the world’s oldest underground is enabling workers to be better connected and more productive. Another good example of London harnessing the latest technology to enhance life in our city is our partnership with Google Maps, which is working to make cycling safer. We share data from London’s transport network — relating to cycle lanes, traffic patterns and road conditions — that Google’s platform then uses to suggest safer, quieter routes for cyclists. It’s a simple, but powerful solution — combining a global platform with local knowledge, to deliver something that benefits millions of Londoners every day.

What could the government be doing regarding technology that it isn’t?

One of the biggest lessons from the last decade is that governments around the world were much too slow to respond to the social media revolution. Of course, the rise of social media has come with extraordinary benefits. But without sufficient guardrails, it’s led to a youth mental health crisis, a surge in online harms and abuse, a dangerous rise in misinformation and disinformation, and an erosion of trust in democratic institutions. As leaders, we have a responsibility to seize the opportunities of new technology, but also protect people against the dangers of it, and it’s incumbent on us to learn from past mistakes. National governments must work proactively with tech developers to make sure that new technologies like AI are used in a way that benefits our societies.

One of the things I’m most concerned about is the impact AI could have on London’s labor market. AI has the potential to be exceptionally helpful to many workers, and can lead to the creation of new high-quality jobs, but it also has the potential to eliminate jobs in some sectors and lead to an unprecedented concentration of wealth and power in the hands of a privileged few. That’s why we’ve launched the London AI and Jobs Taskforce — bringing together experts from across business, government, trade unions and the tech sector to better understand how work is changing in our city, and what action we need to take to protect jobs and livelihoods.

What book most shaped your conception of the future?

I really enjoyed the Booker Prize-winning Orbital by Samantha Harvey, which follows astronauts aboard the International Space Station looking back at Earth from orbit as borders disappear. What struck me most is that its vision of the future is not driven by technological triumphalism or the idea of escaping Earth, but by the need to work together more thoughtfully to protect and improve the world we already share.

That resonates strongly with how I think about emerging technologies like AI. The most important impacts of technological change are not abstract or distant. They are felt in our everyday lives. Orbital captures the idea that progress only has meaning if it ultimately serves humanity and strengthens our collective responsibility to one another.

What has surprised you the most this year?

AI is here, now — radically reshaping the way we live and work. And yet, the way we’re responding to it still feels much too fragmented and slow.

Former New York City Mayor Mike Bloomberg once said that mayors have often been the first to drive progress on global challenges — even as national and international responses lag behind. He’s right — from air pollution to climate change, time and again city leaders have been the ones to step up and drive progress, and now we’re doing it again [with AI].
David Sacks intervenes in AI executive order

Former AI czar David Sacks raised objections to an executive order on AI shortly before it was set to be signed, POLITICO’s Sophia Cai, Cheyenne Haslett and Jacob Wendler report.

President Donald Trump was set to sign an executive order on Thursday to address the threat that frontier AI poses to cybersecurity, which would have included a voluntary testing regime by federal agencies. According to a senior White House official and one person familiar with the matter, however, Sacks told Trump shortly before the planned signing ceremony that this testing would hamper innovation and put the U.S. at a disadvantage in the race with China.

“I didn’t like certain aspects of it,” Trump told reporters Thursday morning, referring to the order. “I think it gets in the way of — we’re leading China. We’re leading everybody, and I don’t want to do anything that’s going to get in the way of that.”

Sacks did not respond to a request for comment.
Hims & Hers under scrutiny

The Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee is inquiring into a data breach of Hims & Hers — a telehealth company that offers care for conditions like hair loss and erectile dysfunction — POLITICO’s Morning Cybersecurity team was the first to report.

Committee Chair Bill Cassidy (R-La.) sent a letter to Hims & Hers CEO Andrew Dudum on Thursday asking about the company’s cybersecurity practices, its communications with federal agencies and other details about the breach. Cassidy also requested information on what data was accessed. Hims & Hers has said limited customer data was exposed in the breach.

“At a time when hostile actors are increasingly using sophisticated tactics leveraging artificial intelligence, it is essential for the health care sector to take meaningful steps to safeguard patient and consumer information,” Cassidy wrote in the letter.

item.title: Why the AI encyclical isn’t just hot air
item.description: Why the AI encyclical isn’t just hot air
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

Pope Leo XIV attends the presentation in the Vatican of his first encyclical "Magnifica Humanitas" on May 25. | Alberto Pizzoli /AFP via Getty Images

If history is any indicator, Pope Leo XIV isn’t just shouting into the void.

The pope on Monday publicly released his first encyclical — a letter that serves as an authoritative statement on matters of Catholic doctrine and sometimes social questions. Entitled “Magnifica Humanitas,” the encyclical extolls the importance of regulating AI to protect workers, curb its use in weaponry and otherwise reinforce human dignity as the technology reshapes society.

The document has attracted particular attention, with unions and tech advocacy groups applauding its exhortations, and industry boosters questioning whether the pontiff is unduly pessimistic. Yet the Vatican regularly publishes treatises, many of which don’t have much impact outside of the Catholic Church, so why has this one provoked so much fuss?

It may be in part because the encyclical echoes, and explicitly cites, one from 1891 that had a tangible impact on politics and policy. Written by Pope Leo XIII — after whom the current pope named himself — “Rerum novarum” championed workers’ rights amid the immense technological change of the Industrial Revolution. It set the stage for the Catholic Church’s involvement in labor organizing and advocacy for social safety nets. Scholars in Catholic theology and history told DFD that “Magnifica Humanitas” could presage another surge in religious activism around AI, with similarly powerful results.

“When you have organized labor … and you put pressure on local politicians and on titans of industry, you end up with not just a random encyclical that nobody reads,” said Charles C. Camosy, a theologian and medical humanities professor at Creighton University. “You end up with a movement.”

Pope Leo XIII’s “Rerum novarum” played a key role in granting labor movements the imprimatur of religious legitimacy. In Europe, where many Catholics resided, it boosted the political power of unions and gave them a doctrinal framework through which to argue for labor rights.

“Rerum novarum” also coincided with the Vatican’s support for worker activism on the other side of the Atlantic. Many Catholics in the U.S. at the time were immigrants, who often worked in jobs such as coal mining and steelwork that had become more grueling due to industrialization, according to Notre Dame American studies professor Kathleen Sprows Cummings.

She told DFD, “The plight of workers in the United States and the way labor unions were working to improve the conditions formed a lot of the background and backbone of ‘Rerum novarum,’ which of course defends the right of workers to unionize and then calls for just conditions and a just wage.”

That encyclical boosted contemporaneous American labor movements such as the Knights of Labor, which had helped to convince the Vatican to allow Catholics to join unions. The Vatican also lent its support and was in contact with Catholic worker advocates like Knights of Labor leader Terence V. Powderly and Saint Frances Cabrini. Catholic leaders were instrumental in organizing strikes and collective bargaining at the time. “[The encyclical’s] legacy in both a theoretical sense, but also in a practical sense, is that it gave shape to a model by which Catholics could engage in politics,” said Touro University law and religion professor Zachary R. Calo.

“Rerum novarum” had a lasting impact on worker protections. Janine Giordano Drake, a religious history professor at Indiana University Bloomington, notes that the American Federation of Labor drew considerably from the encyclical in setting its priorities.

“Because [AFL’s leaders] knew there were so many people with Catholic backgrounds who are laborers, they strategically decided that the goals of the American Federation of Labor are going to be a living wage, [time] off once a week, better working conditions,” she told DFD. “The goals of the American Federation of Labor are really defined around what ‘Rerum novarum’ says.”

AFL-CIO, the union’s successor, recently released a statement in support of “Magnifica Humanitas.”

The encyclical also influenced policy itself. Taking inspiration from “Rerum novarum,” Monsignor John Ryan wrote the book “A Living Wage,” which in turn influenced the framers of the New Deal. “John Ryan really took the principles of ‘Rerum novarum’ and further developed it into the concept of a just wage,” said Cummings.

So could Pope Leo XIV's “Magnifica Humanitas” set off a similar era of Catholic advocacy concerning AI?

Cummings notes that Catholics occupy a different position within society than they did during the Industrial Revolution. “Catholics in the United States are comparatively much more powerful and more numerous than they were in the late 19th century,” Cummings told DFD. “They're also, though, more aligned with the wealthy and the powerful than they were, so that kind of cuts both ways.”

The Catholic Church has also built up a number of institutions in the U.S. that it can mobilize to achieve its goals around AI. The U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops regularly engages in lobbying around policy, and Camosy points out that Catholics operate many of the schools and hospitals that AI is poised to disrupt.

AI regulation may be a particularly ripe area for Catholics, says Camosy, because it concerns questions of human existence and hasn’t become a particularly partisan issue.

“I don't think these issues have been really coded left or right the way other issues have been,” he told DFD. “That to me is a pretty exciting thing …. that can maybe protect Catholics and others who want to engage without having to sacrifice the central tenets of who they are.”
 

POLITICO Pro

Navigate policy challenges with confidence. POLITICO Pro gives professionals authoritative reporting, expert analysis and powerful tools to understand the business of government — in Washington and beyond. Learn more about POLITICO Pro.

 
 
Cybersecurity companies raise alarm about AI

Cybersecurity companies that have been experimenting with powerful AI models like Mythos and GPT-5.5 say the capabilities live up to the hype, POLITICO’s Maggie Miller and this newsletter writer report.

“It was very clear to me that this was going to be a game-changer,” Lee Klarich, chief product and technology officer at cybersecurity company Palo Alto Networks, said of testing Mythos. “I would actually say if you asked me today, it’s more [powerful] than I thought it was going to be then.” Jonathan Trull, chief information security officer of the cybersecurity company Qualys told POLITICO that GPT-5.5 “can basically do what your most advanced app security engineer can do.”

Their warnings come as the Wall Street Journal reports that Mythos was able to breach Apple’s MacOS system, widely regarded as one of the most secure in the industry, within a matter of days. The United Kingdom’s AI Security Institute also found in a report that, even given how advanced models’ cybersecurity capabilities are now, the rate at which they are improving is accelerating much more quickly than expected.
The Supreme Court rebuffs Meta

The Supreme Court declined to hear Meta’s challenge to major social media addiction lawsuits from state attorneys general on Tuesday, POLITICO’s Hassan Ali Kanu reports.

Meta had requested in January that the justices weigh in on whether Vermont’s courts have jurisdiction over its platforms since the company has no physical presence in the state. Today’s decision by the Supreme Court leaves standing a ruling from Vermont Supreme Court that the state judiciary has authority over Meta.

The Vermont court based its conclusion on the fact that Meta operates a nationwide social-media, data and advertising business that involves users residing in the state. The court highlighted claims from the state’s attorney general that Meta “has specifically studied Vermont teen Instagram users to increase their engagement.”

item.title: The case against AI personhood
item.description: The case against AI personhood
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

A Missouri bill would have established that AI cannot have legal personhood. | Justin Tallis/AFP via Getty Images

The Artificial Intelligence Non-Sentience and Responsibility Act is a recent Missouri bill that would have established that the technology cannot be granted legal personhood. Known as SB 1012, it contained provisions to stop government entities from recognizing AI systems as having consciousness or self-awareness. In particular, the legislation would have banned the technology from having the legal rights of spouses, corporate executives and property owners. 

The Missouri Senate passed SB 1012 in early May, but it was killed the following week by state House lawmakers after industry groups raised objections. DFD spoke to the bill’s sponsor, Republican Sen. Joe Nicola, about the pushback to his proposal and why humans shouldn’t be able to assign liability to AI. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 

What makes you concerned that people might try to claim that AI has legal personhood?

They're creating these humanoids that look like a human with two legs, two hands, a head and can walk around. We certainly don't need AI robots claiming to have any kind of legal personhood. Melania Trump marched some of these out at the White House. That caused me and quite a few others to have some concern that AI might, at some point, be given some type of legal personhood and rights.

The bill seems partly aimed at ensuring that humans are legally responsible for their decisions — what do you worry about with the prospect of AI being held accountable instead?

Let's just say a doctor uses AI to prescribe medication. Well, the doctor is the one who went to school, who has the degree — not AI. That doctor needs to be responsible. Same thing with a lawyer, CPA or whatever profession it might be. They're the ones that need to make the final decision, have oversight of the artificial intelligence, but also be free to use it as a tool however they want.

Why did SB 1012 specifically include a prohibition on AI systems being considered spouses or domestic partners?

Marriage is between two humans. It's not between a human and a machine. And we've already seen cases of this happening in parts of the country, whether it's legal or not. Around Valentine's Day, there was a bar in New York where you could come and bring your device and have an intimate relationship with your AI at this romantic dinner. People are free to use it however they want. But when we get into the legal aspect of marriage, if you are able to marry your AI device, then that AI device would end up having rights as a spouse.

The bill states that government entities cannot “consider an AI system to possess consciousness, self-awareness, or similar traits of living beings.” Would that provision have had concrete legal implications, or is that more a statement of values?

It's more a statement of values, to continue to say these machines are not legal entities. They're just tools, just like a cell phone or a computer. It's not something that should have any legal constitutional rights. Constitutional rights are for human beings. Animals don't even have constitutional rights.

Why do you think the bill was killed?

I think there were powers that be that didn't want to see it happen, and they got to the legislators, especially on the House side. I had a lot of resistance to it on the Senate side, the White House pushed back on it. President Trump has an executive order to prohibit states from regulating AI, which I think is unconstitutional. I believe in the 10th Amendment and state's rights and state sovereignty.

I would prefer the U.S. Congress to pass a law, so we would have regulation across the nation. Google and Meta and Microsoft and all these companies wouldn't have to deal with 50 separate different rules and laws, but Congress has failed to act. And for whatever reason, there's a ton of resistance to getting any kind of guidelines or guardrails for artificial intelligence.
New York enacts kids online safety protections

New York is establishing new safeguards to protect kids on social media and online gaming platforms, POLITICO’s Madina Touré reports.

The state’s Transportation, Economic Development and Environmental Conservation Article bill, which was signed on Tuesday, includes provisions that obligate online platforms to block strangers from messaging kids or viewing their profiles by default. The bill, which is part of New York’s budget legislation, also requires that users under the age of 13 get parental permission to connect to other peoples’ accounts on platforms and disables AI chatbot features for kids. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) included the provisions in a budget agreement announced in early May.

“We think we've struck the right balance in preserving youth independence and youth autonomy while still allowing for guardrails to protect against some people who we know are intent on doing some bad things to kids and young people,” said state Sen. Andrew Gounardes (D), who sponsored legislation that inspired Hochul’s proposal.
Nuclear companies score plutonium

The Department of Energy has entered into a preliminary agreement with five companies to repurpose weapons-grade plutonium for advanced nuclear reactors, POLITICO’s Pavan Acharya reports.

If finalized, the agreement would distribute the government’s extra plutonium from the Cold War for nuclear energy fuel, according to a DOE spokesperson. Standard Nuclear, Exodys Energy, SHINE Technologies, Flibe Energy and Oklo were the companies selected for the initiative. Democrats have criticized this plutonium transfer as contravening longstanding U.S. nuclear security policy.

A spokesperson for the DOE’s Office of Nuclear Energy said, “The Surplus Plutonium Utilization Program is anticipated to help companies unlock the next level of private funding to broaden domestic nuclear fuel supplies, spur innovation on American recycling technologies, and unlock private sector funding to fuel the nation’s nuclear renaissance."

item.title: Ghost guns complicate the nature of speech
item.description: Ghost guns complicate the nature of speech
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

Ghost guns can be made at home with 3D printers. | Robyn Beck/AFP via Getty Images

New York is wading into a debate over what exactly constitutes speech in a world that runs on code.

Governor Kathy Hochul (D) signed a bill on Wednesday that makes New York the first state to effectively prohibit 3D printers from producing “ghost guns” — or guns that can be made at home without a license, serial number or background check. The number of ghost guns circulating in the state appears to be increasing: The New York Police Department recovered one ghost gun in 2021, and 109 in 2024. Authorities also allege that Luigi Mangione used a ghost gun to assassinate UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson in midtown Manhattan.

New York’s S9005B, which is part of budget legislation for fiscal year 2027, tasks a working group with developing technological standards for 3D printers that will prevent them from producing firearm components. It also requires multiple licenses for distributing code that contains printing instructions for firearms.

Digital and gun rights groups have already raised First Amendment concerns that these rules amount to a restriction on the free flow of information. At the heart of the conflict is a question about what kinds of constitutional protections should apply to code. Courts have found that code can have expressive qualities in some cases, though they haven’t settled on how the First Amendment pertains to 3D-printing instructions for guns. It’s an issue that’s likely to arise as states like California, Maryland and Washington also consider ghost gun legislation.

“Once the government gets a [First Amendment] exception based on danger or public safety, then … everybody will want all kinds of speech to be regulated,” said Donald Kilmer, a legal adviser for the Second Amendment Law Center. “We [will] silence ourselves into becoming a degraded leader in innovation and technology.”

The Third Circuit Court of Appeals recently contemplated these issues in a case concerning New Jersey’s efforts to limit the distribution of digital 3D printer files for making guns. In its February ruling, the court concluded that not all code can be considered protected speech.

“[W]hile it is certainly true that some computer code falls under the purview of the First Amendment, purely functional code with no actual or intended expressive use does not,” Judge Cheryl Ann Krause wrote.

The court determined that “purely functional code” is not protected, likening it to an aeronautical chart that’s used more as a tool than as a vessel for ideas. It also noted that restrictions on distributing malware or ransomware can be constitutional.

While the court ruled it did not have enough information to evaluate whether the files in the case were expressive, Everytown for Gun Safety policy advocacy director Sam Levy told DFD that 3D printing code for firearms clearly falls into the functional category.

“Purely expressive conduct, like composing a symphony or singing a song, is very different from [...] code designed to do exactly one thing, which in this case is [to] program a 3D printer to make guns,” Levy said.

However, just because code is functional doesn’t mean that it can’t still transmit ideas. In the seminal case Bernstein v. United States Department of Justice, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals found the government couldn’t impose export regulations on a Ph.D. student who wanted to publish an algorithm, source code and explanatory paper for encryption software. The court reasoned that cryptographic source code was a form of expression, similar to economists’ graphs or mathematicians' equations that are used to “facilitate the precise and rigorous expression of complex scientific ideas.”

“The cryptographic software is in the exact same position as the 3D printer code,” Kilmer contended. “The First Amendment says there is no speech that is inherently dangerous — it's only the conduct that arises from the speech that can be punished.”

On that note, Kilmer argues authorities should only take enforcement actions on ghost guns once they’ve been made and sold without a license. That would avert First Amendment issues, and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives already regulates the circulation of ghost guns at the federal level.

“There's still a federal regulation in place that says you can make a gun for yourself in your home using your own material … you just can't then turn around and sell it,” Kilmer told DFD. “That overall regulation of manufacturing arms for sale is already in place.”

However, New York’s law may also be crafted to avoid constitutional issues, since it’s focused on how 3D printers can be used to make guns. Levy asserted that the legislation targets a point in the manufacturing process that isn’t expressive in nature.

“When it gets to the stage of actual manufacturing, you're well beyond expressive conduct,” he told DFD. “You're literally instructing a machine to illegally manufacture a firearm or a firearm part, and that's not First Amendment protected.”

Jess D'Amelia, deputy press secretary for Hochul, said in a statement: “This legislation, as with all laws in New York State, has been carefully crafted to ensure compliance with the Constitution while addressing the real and growing threat of ghost guns and illegally manufactured weapons of war, and the Governor is confident these measures will make all New York communities safer."
California sues a DNA testing firm

Attorney General Rob Bonta is suing the DNA testing firm formerly known as 23andMe for allegedly lax security measures, POLITICO’s Tyler Katzenberger reports.

A complaint that Bonta filed on Thursday accuses the company now called Chrome Holding Co. of downplaying a 2023 breach that exposed nearly 7 million customers’ health conditions, ethnicity and ancestry. The complaint claims that the company misled customers about its security measures, and paid a hacker’s ransom to take down posts about its systems’ vulnerabilities.

“23andMe collected genetic data about millions of people, failed to meet its obligation under California law to keep that information safe, and then lied to consumers,” Bonta said in a statement. “This is disturbing and incredibly dangerous.”
FCC sends a public interest warning

The Federal Communications Commission released a public notice on Thursday warning broadcasters to abide by public interest requirements, POLITICO’s John Hendel reports.

The notice advises that broadcasters are “public trustees,” so they have to refrain from airing hoaxes, profanity and obscene content. It also notes that broadcasters cannot engage in “news distortion” — or deliberate misrepresentations in broadcast journalism. “Programming decisions by broadcasters must be made in service of the public and be responsive to the needs of the local community they are licensed to serve, not the private interests of national networks,” the notice reads.

This is the latest move by the FCC under Chair Brendan Carr to hound broadcasters over the content they air. Democratic FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez has been critical of these efforts. "The 'public interest' does not mean this administration's interests," she told reporters last week. "Broadcasters should ignore these latest threats and stiffen their spine.”
