item.title: 5 Questions for Mehdi Paryavi
item.description: 5 Questions for Mehdi Paryavi
item.content:encoded:
How the next wave of technology is upending the global economy and its power structures
 

By Aaron Mak

With help from Hassan Ali Kanu

Mehdi Paryavi | International Data Center Authority handout.

Mehdi Paryavi is the chairman and CEO of the International Data Center Authority, a digital economy think tank that focuses on cloud computing, artificial intelligence and cybersecurity. Under Paryavi’s leadership, IDCA has established international technical standards for data centers. He’s also worked with NASA, the governments of Oman and Ghana, and Google to build digital infrastructure. Paryavi recently testified before the United Nations on the natural resource implications of AI, and IDCA has since entered a multi-year partnership with the UN to accelerate the development of sustainable technology. He talks to us about prospective subscription services for intelligence, and the risk of data centers becoming obsolete. 

This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 

What’s one underrated big idea?

Subscriptions. Everything is becoming a utility that you subscribe to. Just like you receive internet service, energy and gas to your home, you will potentially receive intelligence and access to the world through subscriptions. Subscriptions are something that have not really been discussed, but it is the underlying element that is driving the future of much of what you see around you — because that's the business model, and the definition of life as we know it in the coming years.

What’s a technology you think is overhyped?

The technology that's both underhyped and overhyped is AI. AI is underhyped because nobody has a grasp of the extent to which it can impact your life: How it can both improve progress and at the same time degrade your critical thinking, your mental conditioning.

But also, it’s overhyped because the claim is that it will basically do everything. There is a lot of human intervention. We are the ones as human beings who are making AI as capable as it is. We [facilitate] AI learning, so that in the future we can have AI inference. We are the ones as a human population educating AI, providing it the metadata, taking it through trial and error, and the maturity process.

What could the government be doing regarding technology that it isn’t?

The most important thing that governments need to do is to understand technology. They don't know the implications of technology and AI for households, for social bonds, for economic prosperity. They don't understand the infrastructure requirements to uplift communities to be able to cater to AI needs. We need to build computing capabilities and capacities, otherwise we will miss the race. How do you build that without hurting communities, without hurting the environment? Where is the balance?

We need to make sure [politicians] have the credentials, experience and expertise to drive not only the cities and the counties and the states, but also entire countries into the new era. AI cannot run in silos. It needs energy, resources, manpower, submarine cable connectivity. There are so many interdependencies. It is not as simple as: “Let me build my data centers.”

What book most shaped your conception of the future?

Civilizations: Ten Thousand Years of Ancient History by Jane McIntosh and Clint Twist. The future is nothing but a reflection of the past. When you read the history of humanity, you see the ups and downs of empires and civilizations. Arrogance is the number one enemy to any empire. AI can change the way you and I search for things or read things, but it cannot change the human experience. You can follow the trends of history, and the trends say one thing: If you are hungry, passionate, innovative, if you make the right alliances, you will lead the future.

If the technology of the future 5,000 years ago was fire, you could rule if you made the best of fire. If today it is AI, the same concept applies. You still need to be humble and collaborate with the rest of the world, and you still need to be hungry. And you must make sure that you take your population and your people with you.

What has surprised you the most this year?

The biggest surprise was a few months ago when [Nvidia CEO] Jensen Huang said [the company] will sell a trillion dollars of chips. Not many people understand what that means. To sell chips, you need to build data centers. To build data centers, you need energy and a workforce. Both of them do not exist today. We don't have enough workforce to run data centers and the hundreds of gigawatts of energy that is required.

The second thing is … if I build a $10 billion data center around this chip, in one year the chip is going to be revolutionized to a point that this data center looks obsolete. I have killed and depreciated that asset. That creates hesitation in the market.

That was the biggest surprise — the numbers that were thrown around. It will help the economy for sure, and we are one of the pillars trying to make sure that this expansion actually happens. But how do you get there?
CNN sues Perplexity

CNN sued Perplexity AI on Thursday, alleging the chatbot search engine illegally copies and uses the news outlet’s trademarks and copyrighted work to generate answers for users.

The lawsuit is the latest one filed by news outlets, publishers and other content owners alleging that AI companies unlawfully use copyrighted content from the internet to power their generative AI products.

CNN’s case alleges Perplexity engages in “large-scale and unlawful copying and distribution,” sometimes providing verbatim copies of its paywalled articles. The search engine also uses CNN’s logos, falsely suggesting an affiliation that harms the brand when Perplexity produces hallucinated answers, the lawsuit said.

“The public rely on high quality news journalism reported by human beings to understand their world, which is frequently dangerous and expensive to produce,” a CNN spokesperson said. “Commercial operators can and must pay to make use of it,” whether through licensing arrangements or legal damages.

The complaint, which was filed in federal court in New York, adds that Perplexity is knowingly misusing CNN’s materials because a content-sharing deal the two companies had been negotiating over ultimately fell through.

Perplexity rejected the allegations Friday. “You can’t copyright facts,” a company spokesperson told POLITICO.

Perplexity is facing similar lawsuits from The New York Times, Chicago Tribune and Encyclopedia Britannica. Amazon has sued the startup to block its AI bots from scraping up information from its online storefront.

Politico is part of a group of plaintiffs suing AI startup Cohere for similar alleged copyright and trademark violations.

CNN is represented by Rothwell, Figg, Ernst & Manbeck, which also represents the New York Times in copyright actions against OpenAI and Microsoft.
U.S. needles German streaming legislation

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer attacked a legislative proposal in Germany that would require streaming services like Netflix to invest in local media, POLITICO’s Milena Wälde reports.

The draft law, which the Cabinet of Chancellor Friedrich Merz approved on Wednesday, would oblige broadcasters and streaming companies to invest at least 8 percent of their annual revenues from Germany into domestic and broader European film and television projects. Greer said such a law would violate a trade pact that President Donald Trump and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen struck in 2025 while in Turnberry, Scotland, which the EU agreed to implement last week.

“If this tax on American companies is enacted, it would be at odds with the Turnberry Agreement, in which the European Union committed to ‘address unjustified digital trade barriers’ — not erect new ones,” Greer said. Wolf Osthaus, Netflix’s senior global affairs director in Germany, told AFP, “If regulation ultimately makes it harder to invest in ambitious projects and, as a result, fewer titles are produced overall, that benefits neither audiences nor the production location.” POLITICO’s Mickey Djuric also reported this month that Canadian regulators have ordered global streaming platforms to invest 15 percent of their revenues from the country in domestic TV.
